These are the first findings providing objective evidence about the relative ability of consumers to identify, and thus self-regulate purchases of, loot boxes and suggest that parents and non-gamers may require support to ensure informed purchasing decisions.

articles.title: Can monkeys and apes use sequence order to resolve perceptual ambiguity? A lack of evidence in two rhesus macaques and one language trained bonobo
articles.abstract: In human language, word order impacts how words are categorized and understood (as nouns, verbs etc.). We have demonstrated that this effect extends to non-linguistic stimuli, suggesting that the impact of sequence order on stimulus categorization is a domain-general, rather than language-specific cognitive process. Here, we ask if this process is evolutionarily conserved in other non-human primates. We developed a non-linguistic experiment and tested rhesus macaques (Macaca mulatta) and bonobos (Pan paniscus). Participants first learned to categorize shapes (as rounded, squared or pointed). We next assessed how they categorized ambiguous morph shapes by combining exemplars from each category. We provided sequential information by training the animals to select shapes in a specified order: rounded, then squared and then pointed. Finally, we assessed whether presentation in specific positions in this learned sequence would impact subsequent categorization of ambiguous morph shapes. In humans, an ambiguous morph was more likely to be categorized as the shape it replaced in a sequence. Non-human primates, however, showed no such effect, categorizing stimuli independent of their position in a sequence. This suggests that the tendency to infer category membership from sequence order is not shared across primates, and may have evolved more recently in the human lineage.

articles.title: Circularly polarized luminescence as a contingency assay for ‘mirror life’ bio-hazards
articles.abstract: Mirror life presents a low-likelihood but high-severity global biosecurity threat that has attracted the attention of bioscientists, governments and international security organizations. However, current analytical techniques are not fit to identify mirror life biohazards. Herein, we propose the first assay method for screening against mirror life. This approach is based upon optical circularly polarized luminesce (CPL) signatures generated by fluorescent probes, which bind to subcellular targets (e.g. membranes, organelles, nucleic acids, etc.). Probes can either be achiral or be intrinsically chiral. We set out why a multi-probe reporter panel approach incorporating many CPL-generating probes is necessary to identify mirror life with a high degree of confidence (i.e. avoiding false positives). The distinct CPL signatures can be analysed via recent innovations in CPL detection, i.e. rapid CPL spectroscopy, CPL microscopy (enantioselective differential chiral contrast, EDCC, imaging) and CPL EDCC cameras. While these are advanced technologies, they share the same fundamental optical principles as three-dimensional cinema glasses and so are amenable to scaling and portable applications. The CPL assay approach to mirror life screening could be a useful tool for screening against mirror life biohazards and ensuring compliance with any potential future international legislation against mirror-life research.

articles.title: Code-driven planning in grid worlds with large language models
articles.abstract: We propose an iterative programmatic planning (IPP) framework that solves grid-based tasks by using large language models (LLMs) to synthesize interpretable, executable programs that act as agent policies mapping environment states to action sequences, rather than relying on traditional search or reinforcement learning. Alongside prompting strategies such as direct code generation, pseudocode conditioned refinement and curriculum-based prompting, IPP centres on an iterative refinement mechanism that updates code from coarse, task-level feedback. We evaluate our approach using six leading LLMs and two challenging grid-based benchmarks (grid-based reasoning for assessing spatial planning (GRASP) and MiniGrid). Our IPP framework demonstrates improvements over direct code generation for five of the six models, with net energy gains ranging from a few per cent to roughly threefold and, for Gemini-2.5-Pro, a sign flip from a negative baseline to a strongly positive score, establishes a new state-of-the-art result for GRASP and significantly outperforms direct elicitation from GPT-o3-mini (by 43% on the hardest MiniGrid task to 116% on GRASP). While code generation has a higher initial prompting cost compared to direct solution elicitation ($0.08 per task versus $0.002 per instance for GPT-o3-mini), the code can be reused for any number of instances, making the amortized cost significantly lower (by 400 times on GPT-o3-mini across the complete GRASP benchmark). Beyond performance gains, IPP produces reusable, human-readable policies that support transparent inspection and modification, underscoring the advantages of planning as program synthesis over per-instance inference. The code and results can be found at http://github.com/Mystic-Slice/LLM-Planning-CodeGen.

articles.title: Deep time dietary convergence evidenced by the stomach contents of a fossil seal from the Southwest Atlantic
articles.abstract: The Neogene fossil record of Patagonia provides important insights into the evolution and ecological diversification of marine predators in the Southern Hemisphere. Among these, Kawas benegasorum, an extinct seal from the Late Miocene Puerto Madryn Formation, represents the only record of a putative phocine (northern seals) in the Southern Hemisphere and preserves rare evidence of stomach contents. However, its original description was concise, and lacked detailed information on its dentition and stomach contents, leaving aspects of its morphology, phylogeny and paleoecology unresolved. We re-describe the holotype and only known specimen of K. benegasorum, providing the first comprehensive study of its postcranial morphology, new information on its dentition and a detailed examination of its stomach contents. We show that Kawas has both monachine- and phocine-like traits, with an overall morphology suggesting affinities with Monachinae. However, phylogenetic analyses yielded conflicting results, recovering Kawas either within Phocinae or in an unresolved position within Phocidae. The stomach contents indicate a piscivorous diet with coastal, benthic and demersal prey, broadly comparable to that of extant South American sea lions inhabiting the region. These results document early benthic nearshore foraging in pinnipeds and suggest dietary convergence across geological time in the western South Atlantic by the Late Miocene.

articles.title: Differences in post-conflict behaviour in wolves and dog-admixed wolves
articles.abstract: Several species rely on mechanisms to resolve conflicts and reduce their negative consequences, including reconciliation and third-party affiliation (i.e. post-conflict affiliative interactions between victims and aggressors, and between victims and third parties, respectively). Here, we studied reconciliation and third-party affiliation in two groups of wolves (n = 20) and three groups of wolves introgressed with dogs (i.e. second- or later-generation backcrosses of wolf-dog hybrids to wolves; n = 13), in captivity. We conducted behavioural observations of post-conflict affiliative interactions using continuous focal sampling for 2 minutes following an aggression, and during matched-control periods. Our results showed that both admixed and non-admixed wolves engaged in post-conflict affiliation consistent with reconciliation and third-party affiliation. Although we found no evidence that admixed wolves showed lower reconciliation or third-party affiliation than non-admixed wolves, social factors had different modulatory effects in admixed and non-admixed wolves. In particular, stronger social bonds promoted post-conflict affiliation in non-admixed wolves, whereas greater rank distance was associated with higher post-conflict affiliation in admixed wolves. Moreover, post-conflict affiliation was more likely following high-intensity aggression in both admixed and non-admixed wolves, and after unidirectional conflicts in the latter. These findings indicate that dog introgression may influence post-conflict behaviour in wolves and suggest that, while both admixed and non-admixed wolves engage in post-conflict affiliation, the mechanisms underlying them may partially differ.

articles.title: Early-life experience and disease exposure affect pathogen avoidance behaviour in macaques
articles.abstract: Pathogens exert strong selective pressure on group-living primates. In humans, disease defence includes both a biological and behavioural immune system, which includes the emotion of disgust and avoidance behaviours shaped by genetics, learning and culture. While pathogen avoidance is documented in nonhuman primates, little is known about how ecological and developmental factors influence pathogen sensitivity, that is, individual variation in pathogen avoidance. We conducted two studies to examine this in macaques. Our first study tested macaques (n = 54) from seven different species and four different rearing backgrounds in a visual food-choice task where food was either placed on a substrate with or without pathogenic cues. Macaques preferred feeding on non-contaminated substrates, with sanctuary-born individuals showing greater avoidance than former pets. Our second study tested sanctuary-born Japanese macaques (n = 55) from four groups; three groups had recently experienced an infectious disease outbreak. Macaques from exposed groups showed significantly higher avoidance of contaminated substrates. Together, our findings suggest that early life rearing experience and recent disease exposure shape pathogen sensitivity in macaques, demonstrating a flexible behavioural immune system in Old World monkeys. These findings suggest that flexible, context-sensitive pathogen avoidance is present in Old World monkeys, providing the behavioural foundations from which human disgust may have evolved.

articles.title: Eco-geomorphic response of the Funafuti Atoll reef flat, central Pacific, to sea-level rise and tropical storms over 120 years (1898–2019)
articles.abstract: This study examines eco-geomorphic changes on the exposed reef flat of Funafuti Atoll over the past 120 years to assess the relative influence of sea-level rise and storm events on reef flat and adjacent environments. Despite a documented sea-level rise of approximately 0.45 m during this period, we find no evidence of long-term structural or ecological alteration on the reef flat itself. We attribute this stability to emergent properties that may buffer against sea-level–driven impacts observed elsewhere. By contrast, significant geomorphic adjustments occurred at the reef flat margins: spur destruction on the seaward edge and increased island elevation landward. These changes reflect cyclone-induced disturbances combined with relative submergence of the reef flat. Notably, this research provides the first empirical evidence linking rising sea levels to increased atoll island elevation. Our findings suggest that future trajectories of reef flats and islands will depend on site-specific interactions among eco-geomorphic inheritance, sea-level rise rates and storm frequency. While these results are broadly applicable to emergent reef flats typical of Indo-Pacific atolls, further comparative studies across diverse reef flat types are essential to refine predictions of atoll resilience under accelerating climate change.

articles.title: Experience-dependent shifts in behavioural decision-making following repeated captures in a wild mammal
articles.abstract: Live trapping is central to behavioural ecology, yet whether post-capture behaviour reflects consistent among-individual differences and how it is modified by repeated captures remain poorly understood. Here, we repeatedly captured wild individuals of the rodent Apodemus mystacinus and temporarily held them in a standardised wooden experimental box. We then allowed them to voluntarily exit the box near the capture location and continuously recorded their behaviour for 5 minutes. Using multilevel, multivariate and continuous-time multi-state models, we characterise the sequence of behavioural states from confinement to escape. We also test whether capture experience reorganises individual behavioural trajectories and whether individual characteristics, such as body mass and sex, mediate behavioural transitions across capture–recapture events. We show that there is among-individual variation in the measured post-capture behaviours and that repeated captures reorganise the structure and sequential organisation of behavioural responses after individuals exit a trap. Importantly, we also show that recapture experience and body mass are associated with an increased tendency towards rapid escape. In contrast, we find that sex has no detectable effects. Our findings highlight that behaviours expressed immediately after trap release do not represent individuals' undisturbed ecological baseline, but instead experience-dependent responses shaped by individuals' cumulative history of interactions with their environment.

articles.title: Have you really seen this illusory face before? Illusory faces bias recognition memory reports
articles.abstract: Visual memory is known to be influenced by objective image properties, including image size and contrast, as well as visual category. However, the influence of illusory perceptual experience on memory remains less understood. Here we investigated whether face pareidolia, a robust illusory phenomenon where certain stimuli elicit a face-like percept despite not being real faces, influences memory. While we assumed illusory faces would be remembered better than matched control images since they are surprising, interesting, draw more attention and may be associated with longer observation times, old-new recognition memory sensitivity was not consistently influenced by the face illusion. Surprisingly, decision criterion was more liberal for illusory faces than for other categories, and this effect scaled with illusory strength such that participants were more likely to report having seen illusory faces for stronger illusory face percepts. In a two-alternative-forced-choice recognition memory paradigm that minimizes criterion influence, we found that the tendency to report having seen illusory faces is present even for unseen images. Further analyses, involving confidence ratings indicated our findings probably reflect a heightened sense of familiarity for illusory faces and not genuine false memory. Our results suggest that during retrieval, illusory faces influence decisions independently of the actual memory trace.

articles.title: How methodological cues shape trust in psychological research and legal judgements: a vignette study
articles.abstract: Over the past decade, psychology has embraced transparency and reproducibility reforms to address the replication crisis, raising the question of whether these signals help legal decision makers identify reliable psychological evidence. This study examines how these reforms influence perceived study reliability and downstream decision-making. We hypothesized that higher methodological quality (larger sample sizes, preregistration, and replications or meta-analyses) would increase perceived reliability and influence guilt judgements. We conducted an online vignette experiment, including individuals with doctorates and laypersons, who evaluated fictitious legal cases accompanied by research summaries varying in sample size (low versus high), preregistration status (preregistered versus not) and study design (primary study versus replication versus meta-analysis). Larger sample sizes consistently enhanced perceived reliability across both groups, whereas preregistration did not. Doctorate participants rated replications and meta-analyses as more reliable than primary studies; laypersons did not differentiate among designs. Importantly, none of the methodological quality cues influenced guilt judgements, despite shaping reliability judgements. This suggests that recognizing methodological quality alone may not shape downstream decisions. Future research should replicate the evidence in more ecologically valid legal designs (e.g. expert testimony) and with a broader range of methodological indicators to better understand how methodological quality influences perceived reliability and applied reasoning.

articles.title: Identifying irregular gasoline and ethanol blends in Brazil using a Love-wave sensor
articles.abstract: The quality control of commercial fuels is of paramount importance for ensuring regulatory compliance, engine performance and consumer protection. In Brazil, the composition of gasoline and anhydrous ethanol fuel blends is subject to specific regulatory requirements, and deviations from the prescribed proportions may compromise fuel quality and facilitate economically motivated adulteration. This study proposes a preliminary methodology for the identification of irregularities in binary gasoline and anhydrous ethanol fuel blends based on a Love-wave sensor. The proposed approach exploits the multiphysics response of the sensor to variations in the physicochemical properties of the liquid mixtures, which are directly influenced by their volumetric composition. The results demonstrate that changes in the proportions of the constituent liquids produce distinguishable variations in the sensor response, enabling the identification of different blend compositions. The proposed methodology therefore demonstrates the feasibility of employing Love-wave sensors as a rapid and potentially field-deployable screening tool for the preliminary assessment of irregular fuel blends in Brazil. Such an approach may contribute to more efficient fuel quality surveillance by reducing analysis time and operational costs while supporting subsequent confirmatory analyses using conventional laboratory techniques.

articles.title: Information-geometric optimization of transient dynamics in gene regulatory networks
articles.abstract: The dynamics of gene regulatory networks (GRNs) is governed by the interaction between deterministic biochemical reactions and molecular noise. To understand how GRNs process information during cell state transitions, we study stochastic dynamics derived from a Boolean network model via its representation on the parameter space of Gaussian distributions, equipped with the Fisher information metric. Restricting our analysis to transitions towards a single attractor, this reformulation reveals that dynamics along the gradient flows of the Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence requires isotropic decay rates across all nodes, and that the noise intensity quantitatively determines the potential differentiation between the initial and final states. Furthermore, we show that the Fisher geodesics, previously identified with minimal biological cost, would require the suppression of noise and lead to deterministic dynamics that lacks biological relevance. This suggests that some departure from minimal cost is necessary for cell differentiation. Our approach frames noise and decay rates as fundamental control parameters, providing a geometric principle for the analysis and design of synthetic networks.

articles.title: Lateral palatal foramina are ubiquitous across fossil whales and shared with hippos
articles.abstract: Lateral palatal foramina have been proposed as osteological correlates for baleen in fossil mysticetes. A recent study reported significantly elevated foramina counts in extant mysticetes relative to terrestrial artiodactyls (Ekdale et al. 2024 Sci. Rep. 14, 10174 (doi:10.1038/s41598-024-60673-8)). However, that analysis drew conclusions about fossil taxa despite not including any fossil taxa in its analysis. Here, we merge the datasets of Peredo et al. (Peredo et al. 2022 Sci. Rep. 12, 11448 (doi:10.1038/s41598-022-15684-8)) and Ekdale et al. (Ekdale et al. 2024 Sci. Rep. 14, 10174 (doi:10.1038/s41598-024-60673-8)) and add palatal foramina counts for eight stem mysticetes, producing a combined dataset of 195 specimens. Stem mysticetes are statistically indistinguishable from terrestrial artiodactyls in the number of palatal foramina (stem mysticete median = 4; artiodactyl median = 3) and significantly different from extant mysticetes (median = 46.5). Finer taxonomic analysis reveals that the elevated mysticete signal is driven by Balaenopteroidea. Balaenidae and Neobalaenidae, despite bearing baleen, do not exhibit elevated counts. Moreover, the elevated counts in Balaenopteroidea are a condition shared with Hippopotamidae, the closest living relatives of cetaceans. These results indicate that palatal foramina counts probably reflect the degree of soft tissue vascularization rather than the presence of baleen. Lateral palatal foramina counts cannot be used to infer baleen in fossil whales, and phylogenetic bracketing remains the most defensible framework for inferring baleen in fossil cetaceans.

articles.title: Life stage shapes condition-dependent foraging under predation risk in an electric fish
articles.abstract: Low body condition can promote risky foraging, but whether condition dependence differs across life stages remains unclear. Using field and laboratory studies, we tested whether residual body condition (RBC) predicted foraging under moonlight-mediated predation risk in the Amazonian sand knifefish, Gymnorhamphichthys rondoni. This species has a 2-year lifespan and a single late second-year breeding season. Because adults have less time than juveniles to recover condition before breeding, we predicted stronger condition dependence in adults. Among wild fish pooled across life stages, stomach fullness increased overnight on dark (lower-risk) but not bright moonlit (higher-risk) nights, when most stomachs were empty and non-empty stomachs occurred mainly in low-RBC fish. In experiments under laboratory-recreated moonlight, lower-RBC adults were active longer than higher-RBC adults on full-moon nights, as quantified by electric organ discharge rate. RBC did not predict adult activity on new-moon nights or juvenile activity on full- or new-moon nights. A full-moon interaction model showed a significantly stronger RBC–activity relationship in adults than in juveniles. In light-ramping trials, lower-RBC adults remained active at higher illuminance before hiding, whereas most juveniles did not hide. Our results are consistent with the asset-protection prediction of stronger condition-dependent risk-taking in adults facing late-life constraints than in juveniles.

articles.title: Metabolic features of enantiornithines (Avialae: Ornithothoraces): evidence supporting a semi-precocial/precocial developmental trajectory
articles.abstract: The enantiornithes, a group of Mesozoic birds, have morphological features suggesting a precocial mode of development; however, their detailed physiological characteristics, particularly hatchling metabolic rates, have yet to be explored. Here, we retrodicted metabolic rates for four Lower Cretaceous enantiornithines: one hatchling, one adult from Las Hoyas, one early post-hatching juvenile and one post-juvenile individual from the Jehol Biota, using phylogenetic comparative analyses and a comprehensive dataset of extant birds spanning the altricial–precocial spectrum. By examining vascular density (related to resting metabolic rate (RMR)) and nutrient foraminal size (proportional to blood flow rate) as proxies, we inferred the metabolic scope of the hatchling enantiornithine and determined that it fell toward the precocial end of the altricial–precocial spectrum. The RMR values of the two enantiornithine chicks were retrodicted as 0.67 mlO2 h–1 g–0.93. The peak metabolic rate (PMR) retrodicted is twice the resting metabolism for the Las Hoyas hatchling. These results are consistent with a semi-precocial/precocial development characterized by independent locomotion by climbing using the wing claws soon after hatching. However, flapping flight may have been delayed, owing to incomplete ossification of the sternum, as observed in one hatchling specimen.

articles.title: Modularity without convergence: integrated evolution of the salamander autopodium
articles.abstract: Morphological modularity is known to favour evolutionary diversification by enabling different body regions to vary in response to functional and ecological demands. Despite their remarkable diversity in limb morphology and ecology, amphibians—and salamanders in particular—remain significantly under-represented in empirical tests of modularity. Using geometric morphometrics and phylogenetic comparative methods, we investigate patterns of shape variation, integration and modularity in the salamander autopodium. We first validated a landmark-based method to outline foot shape, demonstrating that image orientation does not affect shape analyses and that species can be reliably distinguished. We then applied this approach to a larger comparative dataset encompassing 149 salamander taxa across major lineages and ecological strategies. Our findings demonstrate that the salamander autopodium is functionally modular: the distal region (digits and interdigital region) shows more evolutionary lability than the proximal pes, while remaining integrated within a coordinated evolutionary system. Furthermore, the combinations of allometric, ecological and life-history factors account for a small but significant percentage of shape variation, with a low evolutionary signal in foot shape. Our results suggest that modular organization of the salamander foot may allow for morphological variation while still being limited by a common evolutionary and developmental history. By focusing on an understudied group and morphological system, this study provides new insight on how modularity influences limb evolution in tetrapods.

articles.title: Moral echoes: do morality and humanness affect emotional and aesthetic responses to music?
articles.abstract: When listening to novel music, extra-musical information about the musician may influence a listener's evaluations of the music. Here, we studied the extent to which information about the musicians’ Humanness, Morality and Sex, conveyed by their vocal timbre and tessitura, affected listeners’ emotional and aesthetic responses to their music. This online, pre-registered experiment followed a 2 (Humanness: Human vs. AI model) × 2 (Vocalist Sex: Male vs. Female) × 3 (Morality: Moral, Immoral, Neutral) mixed factorial design. Participants (n = 400) were randomly assigned to one of four groups, differing in Humanness and Vocalist Sex. Participants read three descriptions depicting a Moral, Immoral and Neutral behaviour and listened to three unfamiliar songs pseudorandomly paired with a description. Emotional and aesthetic responses to each song were measured using validated measures (GEMS-9 scale) and additional items assessing feelings of being Moved, Connected, perceived Beauty, Liking and perceived Creativity. As predicted, linear mixed-effects models revealed significant main effects of Morality for all dependent variables, with Immoral descriptions consistently yielding more negative ratings. Contrary to predictions, we observed no differences in responses to songs based on Humanness, no significant interaction between Morality and Humanness and no effect of Vocalist Sex on responses.

articles.title: Natural recovery and gaming disorder: a case series
articles.abstract: Conceptualizations of recovery in gaming disorder (GD) remain relatively underdeveloped. While remission without formal treatment appears common in longitudinal data, the mechanisms through which it occurs have received little systematic attention. In contrast, natural recovery—the resolution of addictive problems without formal treatment—is well documented in substance and gambling research, where it has prompted broader reconceptualizations of how and where recovery unfolds. Using longitudinal qualitative data from Finland, Slovakia and South Korea, this case series examines how individuals who had previously experienced self-identified gaming-related problems reached recovery without successful intervention explicitly targeting their gaming behaviour. Six recurring recovery pathways were identified: axiological shift, social enforcement, gradual regulation, reflexive transformation, healing comorbidity and environmental transformation. Rather than centring on abstinence or direct symptom elimination, recovery emerged through reconfigurations of life structure, social roles and personal value hierarchies. In most cases, gaming did not disappear but was repositioned within a broader ecology of responsibilities and relationships. These findings suggest that natural recovery in GD may be better understood as a contextual and relational reconfiguration rather than solely as symptom reduction. The pathways identified here provide a conceptual stepping stone towards more comprehensive frameworks for understanding the recovery process in GD.

articles.title: Novel carbonyl iron-mediated synthesis of Pd–Fe magnetic nanomaterials: mechanism and catalytic performance in Suzuki coupling
articles.abstract: Palladium–iron (Pd–Fe) bimetallic catalysis represents a pivotal strategy for advancing the sustainability of organometallic transformations. Herein, we report a facile and efficient synthetic protocol for Pd–Fe magnetic nanomaterials mediated by carbonyl iron, which proceeds without external reducing agents, surfactants or protective gases. In this approach, carbonyl iron serves a dual role as both the iron source and the reducing agent, while in situ generated carbon monoxide provides three essential functions: atmospheric protection, pressure regulation and crystal nucleus stabilization. This unique reaction system facilitates the co-deposition of zero-valent palladium (Pd0) and iron oxide (Fe2O3) onto pristine Fe3O4 surfaces, yielding magnetically recyclable Pd–Fe@Fe3O4 nanocomposites. Comprehensive characterization via high-resolution transmission electron microscopy, scanning electron microscopy, energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy mapping and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy confirms the well-defined hierarchical structure, uniform elemental distribution and controlled valence states of the as-synthesized materials. The resulting nanomaterials display a narrow particle size distribution (2–3 nm), high metal loading efficiency and low lattice mismatch. Preliminary catalytic evaluations reveal excellent activity of Pd–Fe@Fe3O4 in Suzuki–Miyaura cross-coupling reactions. Notably, similar performance is achieved with catalysts derived from other metal carbonyl precursors, underscoring the generality of this synthetic platform for designing efficient and recyclable bimetallic nanocatalysts.

articles.title: Optimizing for happiness in EU technology policy to repay public subsidies for AI
articles.abstract: Backlash against the artificial intelligence (AI) industry is growing globally in recognition of the high costs and highly uncertain risks borne by society. General-purpose AI systems are sold predominantly on the basis of economic benefits, with little attention given to social or non-financial benefits. Policymakers tasked with regulating AI while balancing European Union (EU) rights and values with innovation and free market competition face a seemingly impossible task. A change of priorities is urgently needed in EU tech policy. Current policy predominantly focuses on risk mitigation rather than delivering socially beneficial technologies. EU tech policy should be rebalanced in favour of societal interests owing to the substantial (in)direct subsidies paid to support the AI industry via tax breaks, public funding, privileged access to public lands, resources, data and infrastructure and widespread deregulation. We propose adding a third goal to rebalance EU AI policy-making: happiness. When policymakers are deciding whether subsidies should be granted for the AI industry, they should require companies to concretely predict measurable benefits for happiness, and hold them accountable for delivering on their predictions. To unpack this proposal, we examine decades of research in psychology to identify key determinants of happiness, focusing on three widely accepted traits: relatedness, competence and autonomy.

articles.title: Overcoming barriers to sustainable agricultural intensification
articles.abstract: Sustainably closing agricultural yield gaps remains a central challenge for advancing global food security while conserving biodiversity. This article develops a theoretical perspective on why sustainable intensification (SI) is limited in many lower-income countries, despite the technological feasibility of improving yields in these places. It explores these constraints to SI through two case studies of expanding commodity frontiers: (i) beef in the Brazilian Amazon and Cerrado and (ii) cocoa in West Africa. We find similar barriers to SI across the cases, including limited tenurial, financial, knowledge and cultural support, community-level risks to investment and cheap land favouring agricultural expansion. At the same time, both cases reveal potential for rapid intensification, as demonstrated by success in selected locations. The analysis helps explain why many promising SI strategies have achieved limited uptake in countries where land for expansion is still relatively abundant. The article also identifies a more optimistic pathway: ambitious economic and institutional reforms, well-funded community-level technical and financial investments, and smart conservation policies could unlock joint gains for food security and biodiversity. Global policy and finance changes have opened windows for this coordinated policy agenda, but improved demand-side policies are also needed to tip low-yielding agricultural systems onto new trajectories.

articles.title: Preferences for pitch sequence complexity are consistent with an inverted U-shape in humans and parrots
articles.abstract: A well-established inverted U-shape relationship links stimulus complexity and human music preference, with preferences peaking at intermediate levels. We investigated whether preference for intermediate complexity is unique to humans or shared with other species. We compared the acoustic preferences of humans and budgerigars, a species known for their vocal learning and pattern recognition abilities, using a three-option place preference paradigm. Participants were presented with choices between stimuli of different, computationally defined complexity: pitch sequences with tones arranged either randomly (high complexity), repeating patterns with changes (medium) or fully repetitive patterns (low). Our results demonstrate that, without specific goals or external rewards, both humans and budgerigars spontaneously exhibit a nonlinear (intermediate) preference profile, indicating a pattern consistent with an inverted U-shape relationship. Because a U-shape relationship may reflect a strategy to seek informative sources maximally useful for learning—that is, for building and refining internal models of the environment—this preference in the acoustic domain may support vocal learning. However, further testing could determine whether it also exists in vocal non-learning species. Because vertebrates show inverted U-shape responses in a variety of non-auditory contexts, our findings may stem from general processes, but potentially depend on vocal learning to translate to acoustic contexts.

articles.title: Self-supporting graphitized palm-branch anodes for enhanced electricity generation from sewage wastewater in membrane-less microbial fuel cells
articles.abstract: A simple strategy was developed to fabricate self-supporting bioanodes from graphitized palm-tree-branch powder for application in membrane-less microbial fuel cells (MFCs). Palm tree branches were graphitized at 900°C, 1000°C and 1100°C, ground into fine powder, blended with bitumen and starch, compression-moulded and thermally treated to produce robust anodes. The resulting electrodes were evaluated in an air-cathode, single-chamber MFC using raw sewage wastewater without external microbial inoculation or nutrient addition. Structural and electrochemical analyses showed that the prepared anodes possessed rough porous surfaces, stable carbon-dominated electrochemical behaviour and improved conductivity compared with an activated-carbon-based anode. Among the investigated samples, the anode prepared from palm branches graphitized at 1000°C exhibited the best overall performance. In sewage containing 5g l−1 sodium acetate, this anode delivered a maximum power density of about 1300 mW m−2, which was nearly 25 times higher than that of the activated-carbon-based anode (approx. 52 mW m−2). Even under electrolyte-free conditions, the same anode generated a maximum power density of about 400 mW m−2, indicating that intrinsically retained inorganic species, particularly KCl, may contribute to sustaining MFC operation without external electrolyte addition. In contrast, NaCl showed a much weaker promoting effect than sodium acetate. Electrochemical impedance spectroscopy confirmed relatively low ohmic and charge-transfer resistances under the optimum condition.

articles.title: Soil moisture enhances the vibrations induced by moving earthworms, especially of detritivores
articles.abstract: Earthworms (Lumbricidae) are moisture-loving soil-dwellers that can be categorized into two feeding guilds with distinct behaviours: detritivores and geophages. Detritivores feed on litter fragments and geophages on smaller litter particles mixed with soil. When earthworms move within and across soil layers to forage, soil characteristics might influence the scale of these movements and their detectability to predators. To investigate the extent to which the detection of earthworm movements and the vibrations they thereby generate is affected by soil moisture, we used an innovative method to detect and quantify vibrations of moving earthworms emitted through the soil. We designed a mesocosm experiment in which we recorded, with a geophone, the movement-induced vibrations of detritivores and geophages in drier and wetter soils. Earthworm vibrations were detected best at 200 Hz and were detected significantly more in wetter than in drier soils. Moreover, in wetter soils, vibrations induced by detritivores were detected more frequently and at higher intensities than those of geophages. These findings suggest differences in activity levels between detritivores and geophages, as a function of soil moisture content. The observed activity patterns are likely to have food web consequences because earthworm consumers relying on mechanoreceptors to detect prey might detect detritivores more often, specifically in wetter soils.

articles.title: Synthesis, spectroscopic study, antioxidant, DNA-cleavage and enzyme-mimicking activities for metal(II/III) complexes with azo ligand–eugenol scaffold
articles.abstract: A newly synthesized azo ligand, 1-((5-allyl-2-hydroxy-3-methoxyphenyl)diazenyl)anthracene-9,10-dione (H-MND), derived from an anthraquinone nucleus coupled with the natural phenol (eugenol), was employed to prepare Co(II), Ni(II), Cu(II), Rh(III) and Pd(II) complexes, with the ligand proposed to adopt a tridentate coordination mode. Anthraquinone derivatives and natural phenols are recognized for diverse pharmacological activities, making them valuable scaffolds for the design of bioactive ligands. The synthesized compounds were characterized by FT-IR, UV–vis, NMR spectroscopy, mass spectrometry, elemental analysis, thermal analysis thermogravimetric-differential scanning calorimetry (TGA-DSC), assessment of chlorine content, magnetic susceptibility and molar conductance measurements, which collectively suggested predominantly non-electrolytic behaviour. In the 1,1-diphenyl-2-picrylhydrazyl (DPPH) assay, the Ni(II) complex exhibited the highest antioxidant activity among the synthesized compounds, with an IC50 value significantly different from that of gallic acid (t = 4.31, p ˂ 0.01). Only the Pd(II) complex displayed activity towards plasmid DNA consistent with partial cleavage in the absence of externally added redox agents. Furthermore, activity mimicking phenoxazinone synthase was evaluated for the Cu(II) and Co(II) complexes, revealing system-specific catalytic behaviour. These results support further investigation into the biomedical and catalytic potential of these metal complexes.

articles.title: The paradox of neutral carbonate budgets on coral-dominated reefs
articles.abstract: Coral reefs deliver vital services via a complex three-dimensional framework sustained by the balance between calcium carbonate production and erosion, or the net carbonate budget state. In many tropical western Atlantic reefs, ecological decline has reduced carbonate production, yielding near-neutral or negative budgets. Yet some reefs retain high coral cover and, theoretically, should also have high net positive budgets, yet often show modest carbonate accumulation. We used the remote reef of Cayo Arenas in the Campeche Bank, Gulf of Mexico, to test whether in reefs under suboptimal (variable) environmental conditions, high coral production is offset by robust bioeroder communities, producing neutral budgets. At 14 sites, we quantified carbonate producers and bioeroders to estimate gross production, bioerosion and net budget states. Despite relatively high live coral cover, mean net carbonate budgets did not differ significantly from a neutral (zero) state, despite a positive net budget (0.7 ± 0.5 SE kg CaCO3 m−2 yr−1) and substantial site-to-site variability (range: −2.3 to 4.3 kg CaCO3 m−2 yr−1). Crucially, this neutrality arose not from depressed biological activity (as in degraded reefs) but from an active equilibrium: elevated carbonate production coupled with substantial bioerosion. These reefs, therefore, represent a contemporary, functional reef state in net stasis. Distinguishing active-neutral reefs, where both production and bioerosion are elevated, from impoverishment-neutral reefs, where both are suppressed, is critical for predicting reef trajectories under environmental change and for targeting management, although near-stasis emerging from high carbonate turnover can appear functionally intact yet operate with limited buffering capacity against net carbonate loss.

articles.title: Variation in cultural attitude, knowledge and individual motivational factors impact engagement and tool use in a field experiment in wild chimpanzees
articles.abstract: Cultural traditions shape how animals approach ecological problems. Over the last two decades, Ugandan chimpanzees (Pan troglodytes schweinfurthii) have engaged with the honey-trap experiment, an apparatus mimicking a beehive, while relying on their cultural knowledge. Here, we compared the behaviour of three Ugandan chimpanzee communities in the experiment, adding a previously untested community, the Mwera South chimpanzees of Bugoma Forest. First, we tested whether communities varied in their engagement with the experiment and investigated whether differences lay in individual or community-based characteristics. Second, we analysed individual variation within the same culture, particularly focusing on the new data coming from Bugoma Forest. We found that only the Kanyawara chimpanzees of Kibale Forest displayed a dedicated instrumental method, stick use, realized in their cultural knowledge and expressed by most members of the community, congruent with the largest engagement with the resource and suggestive of a general positive cultural attitude towards honey. By contrast, the two other communities appeared to lack a cultural attitude towards honey, with no attached tool technique overall. Nevertheless, there were also large inter-individual differences. Notably, Bugoma chimpanzees displayed undescribed behavioural flexibility, using a range of tool behaviours, including both stick and leaf tool use, a pattern never documented before. Cultural attitudes toward resources thus constitute an additional layer to culture in addition to instrumental knowledge and coexist with individual motivational traits in influencing the realization of cultural behaviour.

articles.title: When feathers fell from fashion: unpacking the end of the UK plumage trade
articles.abstract: By the mid-twentieth century, the previously booming bird feather trade was a fraction of what it was in its prime, allowing for the recovery of many bird species. We use a qualitative impact evaluation method to assign probable causality to different drivers of this change, ultimately providing expert-supported explanations of how a large-scale behaviour change was enacted to benefit conservation. We outline a method for applying general elimination methodology plus (GEM+), accounting for different facets of evidence reliability, to generate conclusions on most strongly supported causes of change. GEM+ addresses calls for an increase in impact evaluation in conservation, which will require a range of tools, including qualitative, to fill. Analysis of diverse evidence using GEM+ suggests that conservation advocacy, interacting with broader contextual factors, plausibly contributed to a shift in public behaviour that was instrumental in the passage of the Plumage Act and the subsequent end of the trade. This case study has widespread implications for designing effective behaviour change campaigns, as well as providing a framework for conducting impact evaluations in a range of conservation settings.

articles.title: A continuous confinement-deconfinement transition in a triangular quantum magnet
articles.abstract: A continuous transition between phases hosting distinct excitations—bosonic magnons versus fermionic spinons—is a long-sought phenomenon in quantum magnetism, analogous to the confinement-deconfinement transition in quantum chromodynamics. We report evidence for such a transition in the triangular-lattice antiferromagnet thallium ytterbium disulfide. Antiferromagnetic order develops below T N ≈ 0.53 kelvin. A c -axis field suppresses this order, driving the system into a gapless quantum spin liquid with a spinon Fermi surface above μ 0 H c ≈ 3 T , evidenced by a finite residual linear term in thermal conductivity, a Pauli-like susceptibility, and a temperature-independent nuclear magnetic resonance Knight shift. Approaching H c from above, the scattering rate of itinerant excitations is strongly enhanced, while their density of states shows no critical enhancement, atypical of conventional magnetic quantum criticality. These results point to a continuous confinement-deconfinement transition governed by fractionalized excitations beyond the Ginzburg-Landau paradigm.

articles.title: A phosphorylation-gated GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 module controls drought-responsive transcription
articles.abstract: Drought adaptation requires rapid spatial reorganization of signaling proteins to reprogram stress-responsive transcription, yet how phosphorylation coordinates this process remains unclear. Here we aimed to define how phosphorylation-gated protein relocalization regulates a BpLBD1-centered drought pathway in Betula platyphylla (birch). Drought activated two kinase branches: BpAGC phosphorylated BpMAPK6 at Ser318 within a cryptic nuclear localization signal, promoting importin α recognition, whereas BpCKII phosphorylated BpGAPDH at Thr109, Thr270, Ser279 and Thr298, promoting importin β recognition. Dual phosphorylation enabled coordinated nuclear accumulation of BpMAPK6 and BpGAPDH. In the nucleus, phosphorylated BpGAPDH acted as a scaffold-like adaptor coupling BpMAPK6 to BpLBD1, enabling BpMAPK6-mediated phosphorylation of BpLBD1 at Ser29. This weakened BpLBD1 binding to the BpMYB123 promoter, reduced expression of the drought-sensitivity regulator BpMYB123 , and de-repressed drought-responsive genes such as BpRD29B . Disrupting BpGAPDH or BpLBD1 Ser29 phosphorylation compromised drought tolerance. Thus, a phospho-spatial GAPDH-MAPK6-LBD1 switch couples nuclear protein assembly to drought-responsive transcription.

articles.title: Accessing invasion-competent Plasmodium vivax merozoites reveals antibody-dependent NK cell activation
articles.abstract: Malaria pathogenesis and clinical symptoms arise from blood-stage replication of Plasmodium parasites, which depends on rapid invasion of red blood cells by merozoites. Despite the central importance of this stage, direct functional studies of Plasmodium vivax ( P. vivax ) merozoites remain limited by the lack of continuous in vitro culture and restricted access to viable, invasion-competent merozoites from clinical isolates. Consequently, key aspects of P. vivax merozoite biology and immune recognition remain poorly defined. Here, we establish a robust platform enabling synchronized release and high-yield isolation of invasion-competent P. vivax merozoites from ex vivo cultures. Reversible inhibition of parasite egress using the PKG inhibitor ML10 enables synchronization at the segmented schizont stage, followed by rapid mechanical release of merozoites using a liposome-based extrusion approach. This workflow yields highly pure merozoites with recovery rates exceeding 75% while preserving structural integrity and invasive capacity. Leveraging this platform, we demonstrate that antibody-opsonized P. vivax merozoites activate human natural killer cells, revealing functional antibody-dependent immune responses.

articles.title: All-soft organic electrochemical diodes based on asymmetric active layers for signal isolation in deformable electronics
articles.abstract: All-soft electronics have emerged as a promising platform for deformable and human-centric systems, yet the development of mechanically compliant diodes remains a major challenge due to limitations in material compatibility, device architecture, and stable operation under deformation. Electrochemical approaches offer a viable route to address this challenge by enabling bulk, low-voltage charge modulation in soft materials without relying on rigid junction interfaces. Here, we report, to the best of our knowledge, the first all-soft organic electrochemical diode (OECD) based on an asymmetric active-layer geometry. The device incorporates a transfer-printed ultrathin ion-gel interface that preserves conformal coverage and the active electrochemical architecture under strain. The device achieves high rectification through polarity-dependent electrochemical potential redistribution, with a rectification ratio of up to 2.23 × 10 4 at ±1 V and stable operation under tensile strains of up to 30% and repeated mechanical deformation. This ion-gel-based architecture preserves the electrochemical asymmetry required for diode operation while maintaining structural integrity under strain. Beyond the individual device, the all-soft OECD enables deformable rectifiers and logic gates and functions as a key signal-isolation element that suppresses cross-talk in a deformable pressure-sensing array. These results establish an electrochemical diode platform that combines mechanical deformability, high rectification performance, and circuit-level compatibility, providing a pathway toward fully deformable and integrated human-centric electronic systems.

articles.title: Anomalous phonon selection rules and Raman optical activity in RuO2
articles.abstract: Breakdown of selection rules and emergence of optical activity in Raman spectroscopy typically signal symmetry-breaking events essential for understanding novel phases of solids. Here, we apply our recently developed rotational anisotropy Raman spectroscopy technique to single-crystal ruthenium dioxide—a compound of recent interest as a candidate workhorse material for altermagnetism yet whose magnetic ground state remains under intense debate. Our data reveal a salient breakdown of selection rules for zone-center phonons, accompanied by clear splitting in the angle-dependent polarimetry plots for the two opposite helicity-nonconserving circularly polarized scattering channels. These observations provide definitive evidence of a previously overlooked symmetry-breaking event, involving either spatial or time-reversal symmetry. In either scenario, the underlying mechanism is likely a bulk hidden order parameter, potentially involving multipole moments of Ruthenium(IV) set by the local crystal field environment. Our work demonstrates how subtle symmetry-breaking events can manifest through lattice dynamics and calls for renewed experimental and theoretical efforts to map the phase diagram of ruthenium dioxide as a system poised near quantum phase transition boundaries.

articles.title: BCG vaccination mitigates tau pathology and restores cognitive function in PS19 mice
articles.abstract: Retrospective studies in patients with nonmuscle invasive bladder cancer have reported a significant reduction in Alzheimer’s disease incidence (12 to 78%) among Bacille Calmette-Guérin (BCG) recipients versus controls. To investigate the underlying mechanisms, we evaluated BCG in the PS19 mouse model of tauopathy. We found that BCG administration reduced hippocampal phospho-tau and microgliosis while preserving neuronal markers. In vivo volumetric T2–magnetic resonance Imaging (MRI) demonstrated attenuation of brain atrophy accompanied by increased glutamate-weighted chemical exchange saturation transfer–MRI signals. Functionally, BCG-treated mice showed improved performance in the novel object recognition test, as well as improved body-weight maintenance and survival. Transcriptomic profiling of the hippocampus revealed near complete normalization of the PS19 disease-associated gene expression signature toward that of healthy controls. Flow cytometric profiling of brain myeloid populations demonstrated a reduction in activated resident microglia, but total microglia cells remain elevated. Moreover, an increase of trained immunity marker CD80 on the recruited peripheral myeloid cells ensues following BCG treatment. Consistent with this shift in myeloid state, primary brain myeloid cells from BCG-treated mice also exhibited enhanced phagocytosis of fluorescein isothiocyanate-labeled tau fibrils and increased lactate production. Together, these findings indicate that BCG induces systemic and central nervous system myeloid cell reprogramming that limits neuroinflammation, enhances tau clearance, and rescues cognitive and neurodegenerative phenotypes in a tauopathy model. BCG is a safe, readily available therapy that merits consideration as a preventive agent against dementia.

articles.title: Building digital pregnancies from the single cell up
articles.abstract: Single-cell digital twins connect in vitro drug screening studies with clinical outcomes, providing a new framework to evaluate therapies and advance precision medicine in pregnancy.

articles.title: CCAN forms the spherical shell-like structure in interphase kinetochores
articles.abstract: The kinetochore is an essential structure for the faithful chromosome segregation during mitosis. The 16-protein complex known as the constitutive centromere-associated network (CCAN) localizes the centromere throughout the cell cycle and forms the basis of the kinetochore. Although cryo–electron microscopy has provided a structural model of an individual CCAN unit, how multiple CCAN units are organized within cells remains unclear. Here, using in silico and in vivo analyses, we demonstrate that multiple CCAN units form a spherical shell-like structure in interphase DT40 kinetochores. CENP-T and CENP-N localize to the CCAN shell, whereas the CENP-C cupin domain clusters at the center. Molecular dynamics simulations of CCAN assembly suggest that CENP-C–DNA interactions constrain the orientation of CCAN units, supporting a spherical shell-like organization via CENP-C oligomerization. Super-resolution imaging reveals the spherical shell-like structure at DT40 kinetochores, and CENP-C knockout or expression of a CENP-C DNA binding deficient mutant abolishes the structure, consistent with the simulation-derived model. These findings provide important insights into the spatial organization of functional kinetochores within cells.

articles.title: CREBBP loss drives immune evasion by epigenetically silencing STING and MHC-I in small cell lung cancer
articles.abstract: Most small cell lung cancers (SCLCs) exhibit low immunogenicity and intrinsic resistance to immunotherapy, yet the underlying mechanisms remain poorly understood. Here, we identify CREBBP loss, a frequent genetic alteration in SCLC, as a key suppressor of tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses that drives an immune-cold tumor microenvironment in Rb1/Trp53 -driven autochthonous mouse models. Consistently, Crebbp deletion promotes immune escape in syngeneic SCLC models. Mechanistically, Crebbp loss suppresses Sting and major histocompatibility complex class-I expression by reducing histone H3 acetylation. Notably, HDAC inhibition restores histone acetylation, reactivates these silenced genes, and induces tumor cell-intrinsic immune responses. Moreover, pharmacological HDAC inhibition synergizes with immune checkpoint blockade to suppress tumor growth in both Crebbp -mutant and Crebbp -wild-type SCLCs, with a more prominent effect in Crebbp -mutant tumors. Collectively, these findings establish CREBBP loss as a key mechanism of immune evasion and immunotherapy resistance in SCLC, highlighting HDAC inhibition as a promising strategy to enhance immunotherapy efficacy.

articles.title: Hearing the shape of an arena with spectral swarm robotics
articles.abstract: Swarm robotics relies on robots with minimal sensing and computation that achieve self-organization at the level of the collective to address a variety of tasks. Yet, swarm robotics still struggles with global tasks that require understanding the broader spatial context in which robots operate, such as identifying the shape of the arena in which they are embedded. Here, we introduce spectral swarm robotics, a framework in which robots recover global spectral descriptors of the swarm’s geometric structure through strictly local interactions. To do so, robots emulate diffusion to locally estimate Laplacian spectral invariants, quantities normally obtained only through centralized computation. These spectral values serve as compact descriptors of the environment. In the present proof of concept, robots estimated the second Laplacian eigenvalue, λ 2 , and used it to classify arenas from a predefined set of shapes with distinct spectral signatures. We show that estimating a single eigenvalue is sufficient for one-shot classification among selected confined environments with distinct spectral signatures. We uncovered a scaling law linking swarm size (a global parameter) and interaction radius (a local parameter) that ensures robust estimation. We validated the approach experimentally on two distinct hardware platforms, Kilobots and Pogobots, achieving reliable classification of arena shapes under realistic noise and sparse connectivity conditions. Last, we discuss how locally recovering Laplacian spectral invariants opens avenues for swarm robotics in settings where producing efficient collective behaviors strongly depends on the global structure of the swarm.

articles.title: Reducing energy and air consumption in scuba diving with underwater exoskeletons
articles.abstract: Assisting underwater locomotion with exoskeletons could reduce energy and air consumption during scuba diving.

articles.title: Structural bias enables reliable sim-to-real transfer in reinforcement learning for robot swarms
articles.abstract: Reinforcement learning offers a powerful framework for automatically generating control policies for robot swarms, yet its application to physical multirobot systems has been limited by the simulation-to-reality gap. Despite substantial advances in multiagent reinforcement learning, systematic demonstrations of gradient-based sim-to-real transfer to physical robot swarms remain scarce. Most work remains confined to simulation, and the few real-robot demonstrations lack evaluation across multiple runs and tasks. We show that this barrier can be overcome by embedding structural constraints into policy learning. We introduce attention-based counterfactual policy gradients for behavior selection in robot swarms (SwarmACB), a multiagent actor-critic method in which robots arbitrate among predefined behavior modules—reactive sensorimotor routines such as phototaxis or aggregation—rather than learning low-level motor commands. This architectural choice reduces the variance of learned solutions, which we argue mitigates overfitting to simulation artifacts. Through systematic evaluation on five collective missions using 20 physical e-puck robots (250 real-robot runs), we demonstrate that SwarmACB transfers successfully from simulation to reality, substantially outperforming continuous-action baselines. By progressively constraining policy architecture, perception, and model capacity, we show that smaller, structured policies transfer more reliably than large, unconstrained ones. These findings challenge the assumption that scale is necessary for successful transfer, suggesting instead that principled structural design enables reinforcement learning to produce control software for robot swarms that is both learned automatically and directly deployable in the physical world.

articles.title: A 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that selectively recognizes ergosterol’s conjugated diene uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity
articles.abstract: Amphotericin B remains the gold-standard therapy for invasive fungal infections, but its clinical utility is limited by toxicity arising from poor selectivity for fungal ergosterol over mammalian cholesterol, a challenge that decades of medicinal chemistry have failed to fully overcome. Here, we report mandimycin M16, a polyene macrolide engineered from a unique 5 + 1 polyene scaffold that uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity. Mandimycin M16 exhibited potent, broad-spectrum activity against 11 tested World Health Organization (WHO) priority fungal pathogens. Unlike amphotericin B, which binds cholesterol, M16 exhibited no detectable cholesterol binding and showed no detectable hemolysis, cytotoxicity, or nephrotoxicity at concentrations up to 128 micrograms per milliliter in vitro and after up to seven daily intravenous doses in mice. Mechanistic studies revealed that mandimycin M16 exerted rapid fungicidal activity through selective recognition of the conjugated C5–C8 diene system present in ergosterol but absent in cholesterol, a mode of sterol discrimination fundamentally different from classical polyenes. In multiple disseminated murine infection models, M16 outperformed liposomal amphotericin B at equivalent doses, achieving up to 3.4 log reduction in fungal burden and 100% survival without detectable renal injury by biomarkers or histopathology. These findings establish that the 5 + 1 polyene architecture enables complete sterol selectivity and molecularly uncouples antifungal potency from host toxicity, providing a next-generation antifungal candidate for the treatment of invasive fungal infections.

articles.title: A fluorescent choline kinase alpha inhibitor for intraoperative molecular imaging during resection of canine NSCLC tumors
articles.abstract: Choline kinase α (ChoKα) is a biomarker of lung cancer, is overexpressed in 60% of human pulmonary malignancies, and is associated with an aggressive phenotype and poor clinical outcome. Patients with lung cancer who undergo surgery have a recurrence rate of 30 to 50%, indicating a potential need for better tumor detection modalities. A near-infrared fluorescent ChoKα-targeting imaging agent, JAS239 (λ ex , λ em : 745, 775 nanometers), was developed for intraoperative identification of tumors, their margins, and local metastases. In lung cancer cells, JAS239 inhibited phosphocholine production, reduced viability in a dose-dependent manner, and accumulated in the cytoplasm where ChoKα is active. JAS239 had favorable pharmacokinetics and pharmacodynamics for imaging metastatic lung lesions in mice. In situ and ex vivo fluorescence imaging of primary lung tumors in a canine clinical trial showed distinct tumor identification and margin delineation with a tumor-to-background ratio of 5.0 ± 0.6 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 2.0 ± 0.2 at 0.5 milligram/kilogram. Fluorescence imaging identified a clinically significant event where an occult lesion was found after primary tumor resection. Fluorescence imaging also identified a close surgical margin, which prompted further investigation. Immunohistochemistry for ChoKα showed overexpression in canine lung tumors proportional to tumor fluorescence. Ex vivo human tumor painting demonstrated preferential JAS239 localization with a tumor-to-background ratio of 1.5 ± 0.1 and a contrast-to-variance ratio of 0.9 ± 0.1. These studies establish JAS239 as a safe and effective imaging agent for intraoperative lung tumor detection, warranting further evaluation for human patients with lung cancer.

articles.title: Cas9 nickase–mediated contraction of CAG/CTG repeats is associated with phenotypic improvements in a Huntington’s disease mouse model
articles.abstract: Expanded CAG/CTG repeats cause more than 15 different diseases that all remain without a disease-modifying treatment. Because repeat length accounts for most of the variation in disease severity, contracting CAG/CTG repeats presents an attractive therapeutic avenue. Here, we show that the CRISPR-Cas9 nickase targeted to CAG/CTG repeats leads to efficient repeat contractions in Huntington’s disease (HD) patient–derived neurons and astrocytes and in myotonic dystrophy type 1 patient–derived neurons. The approach was allele selective and free of detectable off-target mutations. Injection of the Cas9 nickase into the striatum of the R6/1 mouse model of HD using adeno-associated viral vectors led to repeat contractions in more than half of striatal neurons. Upon injection, we observed a reduction in the number of inclusion bodies, an improved gene expression profile, and amelioration of locomotion deficits in the open field test. The effects were greater than expected from the contractions induced, suggesting that non–cell autonomous mechanisms may be involved. Our results provide the proof of concept that correction of CAG/CTG repeats can improve HD phenotypes in a mouse disease model.

articles.title: Erratum for the Research Article “Systematic analysis of cellular cross-talk reveals a role for SEMA6D-TREM2 regulating microglial function in Alzheimer’s disease”
Graft-versus-host disease prophylaxis shapes T cell biology and immune reconstitution after hematopoietic cell transplant
articles.abstract: Successful hematopoietic cell transplant requires immunosuppression to prevent graft-versus-host disease (GVHD), a lethal, T cell–mediated complication. The phase 3 BMT CTN 1703 trial demonstrated superior GVHD-free/relapse-free survival for posttransplant cyclophosphamide (PT-Cy)–based GVHD prophylaxis versus tacrolimus/methotrexate (Tac/MTX), but the T cell biology underpinning these outcomes remains unknown. To determine this, 324 patients were coenrolled onto BMT CTN 1801 to investigate the distinct T cell immune reconstitution pathways of these regimens, including extensive evaluation of T cell receptor (TCR) repertoire, via sequencing of 2359 longitudinal samples and 180,432,350 T cells. Multimodal T cell analysis revealed that PT-Cy was associated with pan–T cell deletion followed by delayed T cell expansion from a smaller founder population compared with Tac/MTX. This created a T cell diversity bottleneck, leading to reduced TCR repertoire diversity for 2 years posttransplant. Reduced TCR diversity, more common in patients receiving PT-Cy, was linked to protection against chronic GVHD when patients were analyzed without regard to study arm. Leveraging donor- and host-specific TCR clonal analysis, we determined that PT-Cy–mediated T cell depletion also depleted pathogen-specific TCRs, rendering PT-Cy patients more likely to lack detectable graft-derived pathogen-specific TCRs early after transplant, which was associated with an increased risk of severe infection. This study reveals how distinct immunosuppression strategies uniquely remodel T cell immunity and shape divergent transplant outcomes.

articles.title: Single-nucleotide polymorphism–directed design of allele-specific antisense oligonucleotides for spinocerebellar ataxia type 3
articles.abstract: Spinocerebellar ataxia type 3 (SCA3), also called Machado-Joseph disease, the most common form of autosomal dominant cerebellar ataxia, is caused by a CAG repeat expansion in ATXN3 . The mutant protein is prone to aggregation and exerts toxic gain-of-function effects, whereas the wild-type protein has important neuroprotective roles as a deubiquitinase. Current treatment strategies for SCA3 lack specificity for the mutant allele. Identifying genetic variants such as single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in linkage with the pathogenic CAG expansion offers a promising avenue to develop allele-specific therapeutic interventions, like antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs). To address this, we conducted allele-specific, targeted, multiplexed nanopore sequencing on 79 patients with SCA3 from Germany, UK, and Portugal. We identified almost 200 polymorphisms and grouped them into three haplotype blocks on the basis of linkage disequilibrium. These SNPs were strongly associated with the CAG expansion. Genotypic modeling of our subcohorts indicated that targeting only two SNPs from different blocks could enable allele-specific treatment of the majority of European patients with SCA3. We evaluated 17 candidate ASOs targeting SNPs from different haplotype blocks. Seven of these ASOs caused allele-preferential reduction of more than 65%. A single ASO application in two SCA3 iPSC-derived cortical neurons (AX1, AX2) achieved up to 90% reduction of mutant ATXN3. Toxicity assessments together with RNA sequencing analyses in AX1 did not indicate evidence of toxicity or widespread transcriptional perturbations. These findings highlight that characterizing heterozygosity rates offers valuable opportunities for selective ASO therapies. Our proof-of-principle targeting with ASOs demonstrates the feasibility of haplotype-informed allele-specific silencing in ATXN3 .

articles.title: Targeting ZIP12-mediated Zn2+ signaling as a treatment for pulmonary hypertension
articles.abstract: ZIP12, a membrane-bound zinc importer, is up-regulated in the remodeled pulmonary arterioles of patients with pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH). Genetic deletion of its encoding gene, Slc39a12 , ameliorates the disease in rodent models. Here, we show that ZIP12 overexpression in human pulmonary artery smooth muscle cells (PASMCs) increased intracellular labile Zn 2+ and promoted proliferation. ZIP12 siRNA knockdown attenuated pulmonary hypertension in rodent models. We developed a humanized anti-ZIP12 monoclonal antibody, APL-9796, that normalized intracellular Zn 2+ concentration, suppressed proliferation in fibroblasts derived from patients with PAH and PDGF-stimulated PASMCs, and reduced PDGF-induced cytoskeletal remodeling in PASMCs and contractility in PASMCs and engineered pulmonary artery tissues. APL-9796 showed dose-dependent efficacy in humanized Slc39a12 rats, improving cardiopulmonary parameters after induction of pulmonary hypertension and was well tolerated in phase 1 clinical studies. Transcriptomic profiling revealed modulation of several molecular pathways, including those involving AMPK, PPAR, and PI3K-Akt. ZIP12-driven labile Zn 2+ signaling underpins the pathogenesis of PAH. Targeting ZIP12 with APL-9796 offers a promising therapeutic strategy.

articles.title: The kinase inhibitor dabrafenib halts progression of cerebral cavernous malformations in a BRAF-independent manner
articles.abstract: Cerebral cavernous malformations (CCMs) constitute the second most common type of intracranial vascular malformations. Cavernomas arise because of somatic or autosomal dominant inherited loss-of-function mutations in CCM genes, forming fragile mulberry-like malformed blood vessel structures that are prone to leak and break. Treatment is limited to surgical removal of solitary cavernomas, and because patients often present with multiple lesions, pharmacological alternatives to surgery are needed. We performed a high-throughput screen of 5200 bioactive molecules in programmed cell death 10 (PDCD10 or CCM3)–deficient mouse endothelial cells, coupled to automated image analysis. This screen identified dabrafenib, a clinically approved BRAF inhibitor, as a compound that restored cell-cell junctions and vascular barrier properties of CCM3-deficient endothelial cells. The potential translatability of dabrafenib was tested in acute and chronic CCM mouse models, where it reduced cerebral lesion burden and suppressed lesion permeability. Dabrafenib also rescued abnormal structural defects present in the developing retina vasculature in an acute CCM mouse model. Mechanistically, dabrafenib targeted extracellular regulated kinase (ERK)5–Krüppel-like factor (KLF)2/4 signaling and suppressed F-actin stress fiber formation in human brain endothelial cells, two potentially independent and central molecular processes involved in CCM pathology. Silencing BRAF did not prevent dabrafenib-induced KLF2/4 inhibition or restoration of cell-cell junctions, suggesting that its dual therapeutic outcome is independent of BRAF pathway inhibition. In conclusion, dabrafenib is a low–molecular weight compound that inhibits cavernoma pathogenesis, suggesting that CCMs could be treated with dabrafenib to block cavernoma growth and vascular leakage.

articles.title: Brazilian butt lifts and vampire facials in England are targeted in government crackdown
articles.abstract: New restrictions on “high risk” cosmetic surgical procedures in England have been announced by ministers as they vowed to crack down on “cowboys” putting patients at risk.1The new rules aim to ensure that cosmetic procedures such as liquid Brazilian butt lifts (BBLs), so called vampire facials, and chemical peels can be carried out only by certain healthcare professionals.Cosmetic surgery and other high risk procedures, such as those listed above, will also be banned for under-18s, the government announced. But procedures provided by the NHS for treating a medical condition such as rhinoplasty, otoplasty, or breast reduction could still be available on a case-by-case basis. Facial botox and lip fillers are already banned for children.2Rogue providers found breaking the rules will face new criminal offences and risk unlimited fines or fixed penalties up to £4000.The Department of Health and Social Care said that the new rules would “close a dangerous loophole”...

articles.title: Conflict and climate change are driving food shortages
articles.abstract: The world is still producing more calories per capita year on year, despite a growing population.12 Yet localised food shortages continue to occur across the globe, driven primarily by conflict,34 and also increasingly by climate change.5Conflict affects all dimensions of food security:67 production is affected as land is either abandoned or harder to cultivate and people are displaced; access to markets is restricted; and people are less able to afford sufficient food.4 There are long term negative impacts on health, manifested particularly in the increased prevalence of stunting.8The Food and Agriculture Organization (FAO) and World Food Programme 2026 Global Report on Food Crises identifies 13 countries and territories where acute food insecurity is expected to increase.9 Twelve of these 13 hotspots are affected by armed conflict and violence, and risk of famine is identified in four: Sudan, South Sudan, Gaza Strip, and Somalia.10 More broadly, around 60%-70% of the world’s...

articles.title: Green transition provides a crucial opportunity to finance universal health coverage
articles.abstract: The green energy transition is opening up potential sources of new finance that could be used to fund universal health coverage (UHC) in low and middle income countries. Fossil fuel subsidies—government support that keeps energy prices below supply costs, whether through direct payments, state owned utility losses, or price controls—can account for a large proportion of government spending.1 Reducing these subsidies as part of a shift away from fossil fuels, alongside introducing carbon pricing and capturing new royalties from critical minerals, would provide extra resources for public services. Health systems, which bear current and future health consequences of fossil fuel use and mining activities, have a strong argument for benefiting from these resources, but how much reaches those in greatest need will depend on political decisions and good governance.Fossil fuel subsidies crowd out health spendingFossil fuel subsidies remain large, widespread, and acutely sensitive to international oil prices. When Russia invaded...

articles.title: Living with POTS during weather changes
articles.abstract: I have lived with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) for over 12 years. It affects me every day and no single day is ever the same. Several things can trigger a flare, including changes in temperature and atmospheric pressure. The recent summer heatwaves were very challenging. I had to postpone going to hospital for scheduled treatment as I knew that the lack of ventilation or air conditioning there would make me feel unwell, and this would have a knock-on effect on my treatment response.Extreme weatherBecause of POTS, my body struggles to regulate its temperature, and this makes me prone to heat stroke. I experience sun sensitivity and altered sweating capacity, and changes in air temperature can make me light headed and dizzy. As a result, I tend to not socialise or stay out when it is very warm during the day, which can be isolating.I have found several ways to...

articles.title: Measuring the impact of conflict on the climate
articles.abstract: Greenhouse gases resulting from armed conflicts are a serious problem. Recent wars in Ukraine, Gaza, and Iran have highlighted the immense potential costs of armed conflict to the climate and overall ecological health of people and Earth. The first 14 days of the Iran war alone produced more than the total climate pollution of Iceland in 2024—roughly five million tonnes of carbon dioxide.1 Five years of war in Ukraine has released almost 311 million tonnes of carbon dioxide—the equivalent of annual emissions in France.2 In Gaza, carbon emissions during the first 15 months of the conflict were more than 30 million tonnes—equivalent to the amount of carbon absorbed by 33 million acres of forests in a year.3Although these estimates provide a window into the climate damage of war, still no international climate agreement requirements exist for governments to report these emissions.
