articles.title: A Research Project for Secondary Schools on Urban Plant Ecological Genetics
articles.abstract: Participation in authentic research projects benefits both teachers and students by linking hands‐on field work with experimental biology and quantitative analysis. Plant ecological genetics is especially well suited for classroom integration, but accessible, classroom‐ready outlines are scarce. Arabidopsis thaliana—a wild species in urban environments with a well‐characterized genome and extensive educational resources—provides an ideal model. Here we present a comprehensive, easy‐to‐implement pipeline for secondary‐school–level research‐oriented projects in plant ecological genetics using A. thaliana. The report includes (i) a step‐by‐step experimental workflow for field sampling, phenotypic scoring, and PCR‐sequencing‐based genotyping assays for environment‐sensitive allele monitoring; (ii) classroom‐adapted protocols and quality‐control checks; (iii) background material and a list of concrete, testable research questions; and (iv) downloadable real datasets and analysis templates for guided interpretation. We demonstrate feasibility with pilot field‐survey data from urban school neighborhoods and report outcomes that validate the approach as a proof of concept. Students can learn species identification, formulate hypotheses about ecological adaptation, perform standardized data collection, and apply elementary genetic and statistical analyses—thereby gaining practical laboratory skills and improved scientific literacy. The methods are adaptable to different time frames and resource levels and can be scaled into broader citizen‐science initiatives, allowing classroom findings to contribute meaningfully to ecological genetics research. This project therefore provides a practical bridge between secondary education and place‐based research, fostering engagement with contemporary questions in ecology and evolution.

articles.title: Black‐Tailed Godwits Eat Animal and Plant Material at a Key Non‐Breeding Site at the Overlap of Two Asian Flyways
articles.abstract: Dietary knowledge of migratory birds along their migration routes is fundamental for understanding ecological and evolutionary aspects of bird migration, how migrants select and repeatedly use specific non‐breeding areas, accumulate fuel for migration and breeding, and assess carrying capacity at key sites in the migratory network. Local changes in food availability and foraging habitat have been shown to contribute to population declines in migratory shorebirds. Nevertheless, the diet of many migratory bird populations remains unknown at key migratory sites. We address this knowledge gap for Black‐tailed Godwits (Limosa limosa) by exploring their diet in the Ganges–Brahmaputra–Meghna delta in the Bay of Bengal, a key non‐breeding site overlapping the Central Asian and East Asian–Australasian flyways. We assessed how benthic prey availability changed during their non‐breeding period based on 600 mud samples collected from 120 foraging locations between October 2018 and March 2019. In mid‐January 2019, we determined godwit diets by analyzing undigested remains of 15 feces and 15 pellets collected from roosting areas, and compared dietary composition with benthic prey availability from samples collected concurrently. Polychaetes and oligochaetes were the most abundant benthic groups in the mud, but we did not find them in the droppings. We observed intra‐seasonal changes in abundance and body size of bivalvia, decapoda, and gastropoda, which were the main animal foods found in droppings and mud samples, and were positively selected by godwits based on availability compared to other benthic prey. We also found plant materials, rice kernels, and rhizomes of Porteresia coarctata, in one‐third of the droppings. This finding extends previous evidence of godwits' herbivory in the East‐Atlantic flyway to Asian flyways. Scaling up our efforts to systematic monitoring could help address conservation questions, such as the impact of shellfish harvesting on the carrying capacity of the world's largest river delta for shorebirds.

articles.title: Corn or Climate? Climate Change Facilitated, but Did Not Initiate, the Northward Range Expansion of the Green Jay in Texas
articles.abstract: Anthropogenic changes are driving global shifts in species distributions. Two highly divergent bird species, the green jay (Cyanocorax yncas) and the blue jay (Cyanocitta cristata), recently hybridized in Texas following range expansions. While the southwestern spread of the blue jay has been attributed to suburban bird‐feeding, the cause of the green jay's > 2° northward expansion over the last 70 years is less clear. Climate change has been proposed as a driver, but concurrent changes in habitat and resource availability—including widespread supplemental feeding of deer—complicate interpretation. We combine ornithological records, eBird observations, climate data, and economic data to investigate the progression of the green jay's range expansion in relation to climate and supplemental feeding. The first records of resident green jays north of southernmost Texas occurred in the 1960s. Sustained northward expansion was detectable from 1980 to 2021 and coincided with reduced severe freeze frequency from 1982 to 1996. Severe winters occurred alongside a reduced probability of green jay detections in newly occupied locations. However, range expansion increased during the period with the coldest average winter in the 95‐year climate record and coincided with growing supplemental feeding. We suggest that winter food supply on widespread hunting ranches and habitat loss drove initial northward colonization by green jays. Subsequent warming may have then relaxed climatic constraints once this novel resource became widespread. This potential interaction between novel resources and climate change highlights that different anthropogenic mechanisms may work together to alter species distributions.

articles.title: Cuticular Barcoding—A Novel Method for Host Identification From Adult Parasitoid Wasps
articles.abstract: Parasitoid wasps are important regulators of their hosts and highly relevant for the resilience of terrestrial ecosystems. However, data on parasitoid‐host interactions are scarce and missing for many parasitoid species as parasitoids are mostly collected as adults without host association and rearing of parasitoids from their hosts can be difficult. Molecular methods can thus help to circumvent this bottleneck. We here present cuticular barcoding, a novel non‐destructive molecular approach to identify parasitoid‐host associations from adult parasitoid wasps. We tested our approach by rearing the parasitoid wasp Lariophagus distinguendus on two beetle species, and washing off remnant host DNA from the wasp cuticle to detect the host species using DNA barcoding. Our results showed a success rate of 49%, detecting the host species in 35 out of 72 samples. Samples containing pooled wasp specimens performed equally well as single wasp specimens, which indicates that single field‐collected wasps are sufficient to identify host associations. Hosts could be detected in wasps that were fixated either through freezing or ethanol, which also supports the application of this method in the field. The primers Jerry/Pat targeting the mitochondrial COI gene performed better than the universal primers LCO/HCO, indicating that more studies testing universal primers are needed to establish this method. This non‐destructive method allows to preserve the sampled wasp as a physical voucher for subsequent morphological identification which will be essential for its usage in situ. Our study presents a novel method that enables detection of parasitoid‐host interactions, and holds significant potential for conservation ecologists, pest managers and evolutionary biologists.

articles.title: FishMitoCleaner: Automated Stop Codon Processing and Quality Control of Fish Mitochondrial Protein‐Coding Sequences
articles.abstract: Vertebrate mitochondrial protein‐coding genes follow a different genetic code, in which TGA encodes tryptophan and a large number of genes terminate with incomplete stop codons completed post‐transcriptionally via polyadenylation. These features are often mishandled when coding sequences (CDS) downloaded from public databases are processed with standard tools, resulting in errors in downstream codon usage and evolution. Here we present FishMitoCleaner, a Python command line tool automating quality control and normalisation of fish mitochondrial CDS sequences in five steps: character validation, internal stop codon scanning, terminal TGA detection, stop codon processing and length normalisation. FishMitoCleaner cleaned 97.6% of input sequences in 22 fish species representing 7 orders and all 13 mitochondrial protein coding genes. Statistical comparison of RSCU values confirmed no bias in codon usage analysis (Welch's t‐test, all p > 0.05). FishMitoCleaner is a Python command that allows researchers in aquatic biology and fisheries science to perform rigorous and reproducible CDS quality control in a single command, and clean sequences ready to be analysed in downstream analyses. FishMitoCleaner is also applicable to mitochondrial CDS data from other vertebrate taxa.

articles.title: Local Adaptation With Gene Flow Has a Polygenic Basis in a Threatened Coastal Songbird
articles.abstract: Species that span heterogenous environments often exhibit local adaptation despite gene flow among populations. In such cases, the maintenance of local adaptation is controlled by several factors, including the strength of selection, migration, assortative mating, and genomic architecture. The song sparrow (Melospiza melodia) is a widespread songbird with diverse subspecies, including the coastally adapted Atlantic song sparrow (M. m. atlantica). Despite extensive gene flow with a generalist subspecies, Atlantic song sparrow populations have been found to maintain their coastally adaptive phenotypes. We produced a new chromosome‐level reference assembly for the species and whole‐genome data to explore the genomic architecture of divergence with gene flow and the genetic basis of adaptation in this subspecies. Adaptation in the Atlantic song sparrow has a polygenic basis, with loci under divergent selection scattered throughout the genome rather than concentrated in low‐recombination linkage blocks. Signatures of fine‐scale population structure, limited genomic differentiation, and divergent selection on a small set of genes suggest a role for natural selection in maintaining this subspecies boundary. Our findings highlight the complex interplay among selection, gene flow, and recombination in shaping adaptation with gene flow and provide insights into the genomic architecture of ecological divergence within a widespread, morphologically diverse species.

articles.title: Plant–Soil Feedbacks May Underlie Competitive Dynamics Between Co‐Occurring Invasive Annual Grasses Bromus tectorum and Ventenata dubia
articles.abstract: Plant communities are shaped by interactions among plants and soil legacies. Plant–soil feedbacks (PSF) may alter invasion dynamics and change plant community species composition. There have been field observations of the invasive annual grass, Ventenata dubia, replacing another invasive annual grass, Bromus tectorum, though previous work has not found evidence of competition that would support these shifts. The goal of this study was to determine if PSF via soil legacies and competition are present between co‐occurring invasive annual grasses B. tectorum and V. dubia, and if so, quantify their effects on interactions with these species. We measured aboveground per capita biomass of these species grown in biculture with three field soils (neutral, B. tectorum, V. dubia) over two experimental Phases in a greenhouse. We evaluated biomass in Phase 1 with field‐conditioned soil, and Phase 2 in soil conditioned from Phase 1. We used generalized linear mixed models to determine the effect of soil origin and plant density on biomass, and non‐linear analysis to quantify competition regression coefficients. The linear analysis showed intraspecific competition negatively impacted both species in both Phases, but by Phase 2 interspecific competition was weakened in conspecific soil, suggesting positive PSF. Intraspecific competition coefficients were always greater than interspecific coefficients from the non‐linear analysis across soil origins. These results are suggestive of a positive PSF which may alter the strength of competition between these species in a biculture. Understanding how PSF influences interactions between these species provides insight into how their invasion dynamics may change over time.

articles.title: Same Genes, Different Wings: Wing Shape Divergence Among Castes in a Social Wasp
articles.abstract: Wings play a central role in shaping dispersal, behavior, and ecological specialization of insects. In social insects, distinct castes with specialized morphologies arise from a shared genome, raising the question of how divergence of traits, such as wings, occurs despite genetic constraints. We investigated genetic constraints and sources of variation in wing shape in the Eastern yellowjacket wasp (Vespula maculifrons), combining geometric morphometrics and quantitative genetic analyses across queens, workers, and males. Landmark‐based Procrustes analyses revealed strong divergence in mean wing shape among castes. Males showed greater wing‐shape variation than queens and workers, consistent with weaker stabilizing selection. Allometric analyses revealed that individual‐level size‐shape relationships are weak across all castes, with no caste showing consistent significant allometry across colonies, indicating that size‐related developmental programs do not strongly couple wing shape to body size. Wing shape also varied significantly among colonies, revealing a substantial colony‐level component of wing‐shape variation that may reflect shared environmental, genetic, and socially mediated developmental influences. Additionally, we found that queens and workers from different patrilineal subfamilies differed in wing shape, demonstrating substantial heritable contributions. Our analyses also revealed limited genetic correlations between worker and queen wing shape components, suggesting that shared genetic architecture would not strongly constrain independent caste evolution of wing morphology. Together, these results show that variation in wing shape in V. maculifrons is shaped by a balance of genetic diversity generated by polyandry, colony‐level environmental variation, including environmental and genetic influences, and caste‐specific selective pressures associated with division of labor. Thus, caste‐specialized wing morphology can evolve in insect societies despite a shared genome and genetic constraints.

articles.title: Fluorine-free chlorinated Hückel-type salt for more sustainable and safer all-solid-state lithium metal batteries
Critical constraints to ecological buffering in a rapidly changing Arctic: A long‐term seabird study
articles.abstract: Drawing on two decades of research in East Greenland, this study shows that little auks, key seabird indicators of Arctic ecosystem health, can adapt to rapid environmental change through behavioural flexibility. However, increasing storms and mercury pollution are pushing resilience to its limits, providing an early warning of broader Arctic disruption. Abstract Long‐term ecological studies testing global change impacts are rare yet essential in the Arctic, a region warming nearly four times faster than the global average. These rapid environmental changes reshape ecosystem functioning across the pan‐Arctic and affect the livelihoods of local communities. Seabirds are widely recognised indicators of environmental change. Identifying species‐specific critical constraints is therefore essential for detecting early warning signals of population decline and ecosystem reorganisation. Little auks (Alle alle), the most abundant Arctic seabirds, are key ecosystem engineers shaping coastal environments through for example food‐web interactions and guano deposition. We present a 20‐year study (2005–2024) of an East Greenland little auk population, combining long‐term demographic monitoring with behavioural, physiological and ecotoxicological data. We quantified fitness‐related traits (adult body condition, overwinter survival and chick growth) alongside potential constraints, including parental foraging effort, trophic ecology, winter distribution, and mercury contamination in adults, eggs and chicks. Over the study period, climate‐driven ocean warming, sea‐ice decline, altered zooplankton communities, and increasing mercury exposure reshaped environmental conditions. Faced with these changes, little auks exhibited marked behavioural and dietary plasticity, allowing them to maintain relatively stable fitness metrics in most years. However, sustained monitoring revealed key constraints that undermine this apparent resilience: (a) Elevated mercury burdens may reduce aerobic diving capacity and thermal tolerance in adults and were associated with reduced reproductive performance. (b) Chick growth was strongly impaired during years with increased summer storm activity, which disrupted adult foraging trips and provisioning rates. Winter storms are also likely to negatively affect adult overwinter survival. Together, these findings show that little auks can partially buffer rapid Arctic change through behavioural flexibility, but multiple interacting climatic and contaminant stressors impose increasing, possibly cumulative constraints on performance. Identifying such critical constraints is crucial for understanding the limits of resilience in wild populations and for improving predictions of ecosystem responses to ongoing climate change.

From topology to biological meaning: why plant family classification matters beyond systematics
articles.abstract: Conceptual framework for family‐level classification. Summary Plant family names are routinely used to structure comparative analyses, trait databases, floras, conservation assessments, and teaching. Yet, these names are not neutral labels: changing family boundaries changes the units across which biological patterns are compared, summarized, and interpreted. Modern phylogenetic inference resolves evolutionary relationships with increasing confidence, but it does not by itself determine which monophyletic groups should be recognized as families. We argue that this choice should be guided not only by monophyly, but also by diagnosability, biological interpretability, stability, and practical utility. Recent debates around large‐scale consensus classifications show why these criteria must be explicit. Recognizing classification as shared scientific infrastructure means that family delimitation matters not only to systematists, but to all plant scientists who rely on taxonomic units to formulate questions and communicate results.

articles.title: Recent plant photosynthate as a driver of ecological and evolutionary processes
articles.abstract: Timeline of key eco‐evolutionary outcomes arising from belowground allocation of recent plant photosynthate from shoots. Summary Plants rapidly allocate carbon from photosynthesis belowground via root exudates and root‐associated microorganisms. Here we synthesise recent evidence of our understanding of the consequences of this ‘fast’ pathway of recent photosynthate flux for major ecological and evolutionary processes. This rapid input of plant‐derived carbon to soils shapes food webs and drives processes including soil CO2 efflux, nutrient cycling, plant community dynamics, stability of symbioses and evolution of contrasting modes of nutrition, such as parasitism and mycoheterotrophy. We also highlight how seasonality and anthropogenic and natural perturbations likely determine the magnitude and dynamics of this fast pathway across major vegetation types, but these factors remain understudied. Further gaps in understanding include demonstrating causal links between photosynthate flow and key biogeochemical cycling processes and the capture of photosynthate by co‐occurring root‐associated microorganisms.

articles.title: Insights into two modes of TdT action in human V(D)J recombination
articles.abstract: Terminal deoxynucleotidyl transferase (TdT) is a DNA polymerase expressed in pre-B and pre-T cells that functions in V(D)J recombination to add random nucleotides in a template-independent (TI) mode at junctions between antigen receptor gene segments. However, cellular, biochemical, and structural studies have also revealed a significant, short-length, template-dependent (TD) mode of TdT, in which it takes instructions from a template strand across a double-strand break. Here, we propose that this can occur through an intrachain fold-back synthesis to generate the short inverted repeats at V(D)J recombination junctions observed in early human lymphoid cells and within the adult human antigen receptor repertoire. This duality is also relevant to the functional and structural flexibility observed during the DNA repair process known as nonhomologous DNA end joining (NHEJ).

articles.title: Frustration and topology in the phase behavior of solute-frustrated $q$-clock models
articles.abstract: Frustration can enhance fluctuations and create new and interesting phase behavior. When combined with the ability to host topological defects, frustration can increase the complexity of a system's phase diagram through topological and frustrated topological transitions. To understand the interplay of frustration and topology on phase behavior, we introduce and study solute-frustrated $q$-clock (SF$q$C) models, in which solute sites are added to the $q$-clock model, a lattice model where each spin can take one of $q$ orientations. The $q$-clock model can exhibit spontaneous symmetry breaking and topological transitions, and the interaction between the spins and a solute frustrates the system, in essence by creating a fixed lower bound on the concentration of positive topological defects or vortices. We perform Monte Carlo simulations and develop theoretical descriptions of SF$q$C models with $q=4$ and $q=6$ to understand their phase behavior. We find that these systems exhibit rich phase diagrams that depend on the choice of parameters. In particular, SF$q$C models have a wide range of interesting low-temperature phases, including the presence of strongly frustrated domains and the absence of long-range order. We also find topological effects even at low temperatures; for instance, we find that topological defects can drive crystallization. We anticipate these results to guide the development of materials that take advantage of frustration and topology to tune phase behavior and fluctuations.

articles.title: Exciplex-Facilitated Charge Extraction and Defect Chelation to Improve Inorganic Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Rational molecular engineering of the perovskite/hole transport layer interface offers a promising route to simultaneously address inefficient charge extraction, defect-mediated recombination, and lead leakage in CsPbI3–xBrx perovskite solar cells. Herein, we introduce 2,2′-dinitro-9,9′-spirobifluorene (DN-SBF) as an interfacial molecular bridge to tackle these challenges. DN-SBF optimizes energy level alignment, establishes π–π interactions, and forms exciplexes with Spiro-OMeTAD, thereby facilitating interfacial charge transport. Meanwhile, DN-SBF passivates undercoordinated Pb2+ through multiple coordination modes, including robust bidentate chelation formed by adjacent nitro groups, effectively passivating defects and suppressing non-radiative recombination. Importantly, multipoint coordination immobilizes leachable Pb2+, substantially mitigating lead leakage and improving film biocompatibility. As a result, DN-SBF-engineered CsPbI3–xBrx devices achieve a champion power conversion efficiency of 22.40% along with significantly enhanced operational and environmental stability. This work highlights the potential of versatile molecular bridges to concurrently enhance performance, stability, and eco-friendliness, which may contribute to the development of more sustainable perovskite photovoltaics.

articles.title: Cross-species atlas of bacterial RNA 3′ ends reveals termination mechanistic signatures and evolutionary patterns
articles.abstract: Deciphering the generation mechanisms and regulatory roles of bacterial transcript 3' termini requires large-scale 3' terminus data. We repurpose PATHOgenex, an available RNAtag-seq dataset, leveraging RNAtag-seq-specific read patterns associated with 3' termini to generate the "Bacterminome" atlas, a rich resource of species- and condition-dependent transcript 3' termini of 32 bacterial human pathogens grown under 10-12 conditions. Analysis of sequence elements near 3' termini revealed, along with the classical intrinsic terminator, other known and newly detected signatures, highlighting the wealth of termination-associated sequence elements. Intriguingly, orthologous genes with corresponding 3' termini show different termination mechanisms in different bacteria, often matching the dominant mechanism of the respective bacterial species. Analysis of condition-dependent 3' termini revealed some conservation across species, supporting the conjecture that alternative 3' termini can play a role in gene expression regulation. Our resource, available through a user-friendly web server (https://bacterminome.huji.ac.il), provides a platform for studying transcription termination at an unprecedented scope.

articles.title: Molecular triage and isoform protection safeguard ubiquitin chain editing on DNA
articles.abstract: In an accompanying study, we identify the RPA-ZUP1 complex as a ubiquitin chain-editing machine that promotes removal of RPA from ssDNA. Because loss of ZUP1 causes pathological RPA trapping on ssDNA, cells must preserve a functional RPA-ZUP1 pool to sustain RPA turnover. How this homeostasis is achieved is unknown. Here, we show that ZUP1 is subject to ubiquitin-dependent fate control. ZUP1 ubiquitination promotes recruitment of p97/VCP and ATXN3, defining a molecular triage pathway that protects ZUP1 from premature proteasomal degradation. Opposing this, the E3 ligases UBR5 and HUWE1 define a degradative branch that limits ZUP1 abundance, with HUWE1 restricting its accumulation on damaged chromatin. We further show that cells express a naturally occurring ZUP1 isoform resistant to efficient ubiquitination and turnover, suggesting that isoform diversity provides a protected pool of chain-editing activity. Together, these findings define a homeostatic system that preserves ZUP1 while limiting its persistence on damaged chromatin.

articles.title: Sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation delineates a progression toward the totipotent-like state
articles.abstract: The in vitro induction of 8-cell-like cells (8CLCs) from human pluripotent stem cells (hPSCs) provides a model to study the regulatory principles of totipotency and zygotic genome activation (ZGA). However, the cellular dynamics underlying 8CLC emergence remain poorly understood. Here, we generate a TPRX1-EGFP/HERVL-tdTomato dual-reporter hPSC line to resolve the stepwise acquisition of totipotent-like identity. We show that 8CLC induction follows an ordered trajectory in which TPRX1 activation precedes the emergence of TPRX1+HERVL+ cells, which most closely resemble the in vivo 8-cell embryo transcriptionally. Single-cell transcriptomics and time-resolved flow cytometry further define a continuous transition from the primed state through a TPRX1+ intermediate to the HERVL+ 8CLC state. CRISPRi and RNA-directed perturbations support functional contributions of HERVL elements and HERVL-derived RNA to this transition, while potential locus-dependent mechanisms remain unresolved. Together, these findings establish sequential TPRX1 and HERVL activation as a defining feature of human 8CLC induction.

Mechanistic Insights into the Colloidal Synthesis of Monodisperse CoF2 Nanorods
articles.abstract: Transition metal fluorides (TMFs) are promising conversion-type cathode materials for high-energy lithium–metal batteries owing to their exceptionally high theoretical energy density, making them attractive for demanding applications such as electric aviation. However, their practical implementation is hindered by sluggish conversion kinetics, pronounced voltage hysteresis, and poor electrochemical reversibility. Understanding the structural and chemical evolution of TMFs and the electrode–electrolyte interphase formed during cycling is essential for improving their performance. Monodisperse nanocrystalline TMFs are ideal model systems for high-resolution transmission electron microscopy because their uniform size, morphology, and electron transparency enable representative nanoscale characterization. Here, we investigate a reproducible colloidal synthesis of monodisperse, single-crystalline CoF2 nanorods and elucidate the mechanisms governing their formation to achieve precise control over particle size and aspect ratio. By independently varying reaction time, temperature, precursor composition, and ligand chemistry, we identify the key factors controlling precursor decomposition, burst nucleation, phase selection, and anisotropic crystal growth. These insights provide a transferable framework for the controlled synthesis of a broad range of transition metal fluoride nanocrystals.

Arabidopsis cyclin‐dependent kinases and MAP65 phosphorylation link microtubule dynamics with salt stress adaptation
articles.abstract: Working model illustrating the CDK‐MAP65‐microtubule module mediating salt stress adaptation in Arabidopsis. Summary Plants possess sophisticated regulatory mechanisms to balance growth and stress responses. Cyclin‐dependent kinases (CDKs) are established regulators of cell division and endoreduplication, yet their roles in abiotic stress responses remain poorly understood. Here, using reverse genetics, biochemical, and cell biological approaches, we show that Arabidopsis (Arabidopsis thaliana) CDKB1s contribute to salt stress adaptation through a mechanism involving the phosphorylation of MAP65‐1 and MAP65‐2, two microtubule‐associated proteins essential for cytoskeleton dynamics under salt stress. Loss of CDKB1 function enhances salt tolerance, accompanied by attenuated plasma membrane depolarization and reactive oxygen species accumulation. In vitro phosphorylation assays demonstrate that CDKB1;1 directly phosphorylates MAP65‐1 at Ser‐503. Genetic analyses indicate that phospho‐dead MAP65 variants confer enhanced salt tolerance, whereas phosphomimetic variants compromise tolerance even in the cdkb1;1 1;2 background, supporting a critical role for MAP65 phosphorylation status at these sites in salt stress adaptation. We further found that CDKA;1 can similarly interact with and phosphorylate MAP65‐1, suggesting a potential parallel role for CDKA;1 in this process. Collectively, our findings identify a regulatory module involving CDKs, MAP65, and microtubules that links cell cycle kinases and cytoskeleton dynamics with plant salt stress adaptation.

articles.title: Beyond sanctions: where the costs of nursery pollination are borne
Cell‐type‐specific PIN‐FORMED 3‐mediated polar auxin transport regulates cambial activity and tension wood formation in Populus tomentosa
articles.abstract: Phloem‐specific silencing of PIN3 impairs polar auxin transport and auxin response in Populus tomentosa. Summary Auxin is a central regulator of tree secondary growth and forms maxima in the vascular cambium, yet how these maxima are established remains elusive. Here, we functionally characterized two redundant PIN‐FORMED 3 (PIN3) paralogs from Populus tomentosa to define their roles in secondary growth and gravity‐induced tension wood (TW) formation. We employed fluorescent reporter lines, clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats‐generated knockout mutants, phloem‐specific RNA interference transgenic plants and isotopic auxin transport assays to dissect PIN3 functions during secondary growth of poplar stems. Loss of function of PIN3 paralogs severely compromises cambial proliferation, secondary xylem differentiation and TW development. PIN3 proteins display cell‐type‐specific polar localization with basal polarity in phloem cells and outer lateral polarity in endodermal cells. Phloem‐expressed PIN3 facilitates basipetal auxin transport and is required for cambial auxin response. Upon gravistimulation, endodermal PIN3 repolarizes along the gravity vector, correlating with TW formation. Our findings identify a cell‐type‐specific, PIN3‐mediated auxin transport mechanism that contributes to auxin‐driven secondary growth of tree stems.

articles.title: Drought‐induced plant dominance shift amplifies functional niche differentiation in steppe communities
articles.abstract: Community trait variation (a), community‐weighted trait overlap (b), intraspecific trait variation (ITV, c), and its relative contribution to community trait variation (rITV, d) for all the four examined traits under different treatments (mean ± SE, n = 12). Summary Trait‐based studies on community assembly under environmental change often overlook intraspecific trait variation (ITV), despite its considerable role in modulating community dynamics, which may largely mislead the inference of community assembly. Under simulated extreme droughts in a temperate steppe, we integrated ITV and interspecific trait variation for four key traits, plant height (Height), specific leaf area (SLA), leaf dry matter content (LDMC), and leaf thickness (LT), to examine how drought alters functional niche structure and underlying processes. Drought shifted communities toward conservative resource‐use strategies, reduced community variation in LT, and interspecific trait overlap in terms of SLA, LDMC, LT, and the multivariate trait space, whereas community‐level ITV remained stable across all traits. These changes were driven primarily by diversity loss and increases in the dominance of fewer species, with negligible effects of intraspecific trait plasticity or species turnover. Communities with fewer but more dominant species exhibited smaller trait overlap. Our findings advance our understanding of the paradigm of trait convergence under environmental filtering. Drought‐induced diversity loss amplifies functional niche differentiation, underscoring the critical role of species reorganization through dominance shifts, with little evidence for intraspecific trait plasticity in mediating community assembly under climate extremes.

articles.title: Engineering uORFs in wheat improves abiotic stress tolerance without growth penalties
articles.abstract: Precise editing of upstream open reading frames enabled in situ fine-tuning of gene expression in allohexaploid wheat, thereby enhancing abiotic stress tolerance without growth penalties. Summary Developing climate-resilient crops is critical for ensuring global food security, yet agricultural productivity is frequently constrained by the trade-off between stress tolerance and growth. This challenge is particularly acute in allohexaploid wheat, a staple crop susceptible to abiotic stresses, underscoring the demand for precise gene regulation. Here, we established a simple, efficient, and transgene-free method for regulating gene expression in allohexaploid wheat by disrupting or creating de novo upstream open reading frames (uORFs) via genome editing. Using ribosome profiling, we identified 1199 actively translated uORFs across the wheat genome and developed a dual-luciferase screening pipeline to pinpoint potent translational repressors of positive regulators of abiotic stress. CRISPR/Cas9-mediated disruption of the uORFs in TaCIPK14 and TaGGP1 elevated downstream protein accumulation, thereby enhancing drought, cold, and salt tolerance of plants. Furthermore, base editing was employed to generate de novo uORFs in TaMADS26, effectively downregulating gene expression and improving drought resilience. Notably, both the transgene-free uorf TaGGP1-ACG and uORFTaMADS26 mutants conferred pronounced yield advantages under drought conditions without incurring growth penalties under well-watered conditions. This study provides a predictable and precise way for modulating gene expression, enabling the coordinated improvement of stress resilience and agronomic performance in wheat.

articles.title: MicroRNA 160 controls the auxin response factor–class III peroxidase module and couples salicylic acid and redox signaling networks in the potato hypersensitive response to potato virus Y
articles.abstract: miR160 links salicylic acid, auxin, and redox signaling with the growth–defense trade‐off in the potato hypersensitive response to potato virus Y. Summary Hypersensitive response (HR) is an effector‐triggered immune response leading to pathogen restriction and local cell death. Small RNAs (sRNAs), mediating RNA silencing, have a well‐established role in antiviral immunity; however, their role in HR has not been addressed to date. We applied a spatially resolved sRNA‐omics approach to uncover changes at the sRNA level and the dynamics of sRNA–gene regulatory networks in potato (Solanum tuberosum L.) HR to potato virus Y (PVY). We show that miR160 is repressed in cells adjacent to HR lesions in the resistant cultivar, but not in PVY‐sensitive, salicylic acid (SA)‐depleted plants. Beyond its canonical regulation of StARF10 and StARF17, miR160 controls a broader regulatory network spanning auxin signaling, cell‐wall remodeling, redox homeostasis, and tuberization. Elevated miR160 levels promote susceptibility‐associated traits, reduce thermotolerance, and suppress genes strongly activated in HR. Mechanistically, we identify a novel miR160–StARF10/StARF17–StPRX28 module that links miR160 repression to the induction of a Class III apoplastic peroxidase in HR, with SA acting upstream. Together, these findings establish miR160 as an important regulatory node that connects SA–auxin–redox signaling pathways and tunes development, defense, and heat resilience, and highlight miR160 as a promising target for fine‐tuning tolerance to multiple stresses with minimal yield loss.

articles.title: No need to exceed: tomato ripening is controlled by a small amount of ethylene
Accurate Atomic Correlation Energies and Virial Trends for Correlation-Consistent Effective Core Potentials III: Quantitative Separation of Fixed-Node Biases and Localization Errors in Cs-Rn
articles.abstract: Atomic benchmarks for sixth-period elements (Cs-Rn) are established to sub-millihartree precision under correlation-consistent effective core potentials (ccECPs) using coupled-cluster [up to CCSDT(Q)] and full configuration interaction methods. These references systematically characterize electron correlation, potential-to-kinetic energy partitioning, and combined fixed-node and locality biases ($η$) in fixed-node diffusion Monte Carlo (FNDMC). The valence kinetic-to-total energy ratio ($ξ$) departs from the non-relativistic all-electron Coulombic virial limit ($ξ=100\%$), remaining confined between 25.8$\%$ and 37.6$\%$. The Un-pseudizing of semi-core shells decreases $ξ$ as the attractive potential energy deepens faster than the accompanying kinetic energy escalates. Periodic trends in $ξ$ reveal a $5d$ plateau near 34$\%$, with a lanthanide-contraction-driven maximum in Hf, followed by a sharp decline across the $6p$ block. In FNDMC, $η$ escalates rapidly at the onset of group-1/2 and toward the $6p$ closed-shell limit, peaking at 5.42$\%$ in Rn. Although fixed-node errors dominate $η$ in most sixth-period elements, a locality error inversion occurs in Bi, with Pb exhibiting comparable error magnitudes. Furthermore, core-valence partitioning alters trial wavefunction nodal topology: in Tl, three-dimensional nodal cross-sections reveal isolated toroidal domains that confine walkers. This work completes the periodic-table-wide ccECP database from H to Rn, revealing how pseudopotential choices govern energy partitioning, nodal topology, and the balance between fixed-node and localization errors.

articles.title: Boosting fluorescence and polarization with nanophotonics for single-molecule chiral sensing
articles.abstract: Detecting chirality is essential in chemistry and biomedicine. Circular dichroism identifies chiral molecules through their differential absorption of circularly polarized light. However, its sensitivity is limited by vanishing absorption at low concentrations. Fluorescence-based methods have already enabled other optical techniques to reach the single-molecule limit and could, in principle, also extend chiral detection to reach this sensitivity regime. They are marred, however, by the combination of weak fluorescence signals and low polarization contrast. To overcome these limitations, we leverage high-index dielectric nanophotonics to simultaneously enhance both fluorescence and polarization for chiral sensing. We propose a reciprocity-based analytical framework for a chiral dipolar emitter coupled to a nanoantenna and reveal the different contributions and trade-offs governing the enhancement of circularly polarized fluorescence. Guided by this insight, we tailor achiral dielectric nanostructures to reach a 1000-fold enhancement of fluorescence intensity together with a 10-fold increase in polarization. Crucially, we show that accounting for extrinsic polarization effects in the angular emission patterns of nanophotonic structures is indispensable for reliable enantiomer discrimination. Our approach opens a realistic path for single-molecule chiral sensing.

articles.title: Epitaxial Displacement-etched GaAsSb Quantum Dots Emitting at Telecom Wavelengths
articles.abstract: Semiconductor quantum dots (QDs) are essential components for integrated photonic and quantum information systems, yet current epitaxial growth techniques face significant limitations in complexity of growth, material selection, and density tunability. Here we report a displacement etch technique that enables controlled formation of GaAsSb QDs with emission at telecommunications wavelengths. Our approach uses arsenic molecular flux (As$_2$) to react with antimonide surfaces through thermodynamically favorable displacement reactions, creating three-dimensional quantum confined nanostructures without requiring strain-driven growth or complex droplet-based processes. Density functional theory shows the two competing As-for-Sb exchange pathways to be nearly equivalent in both reaction energy and activation barrier, which places morphological control in the subsequent adatom kinetics rather than in the surface reaction itself. A single process parameter, the As$_2$ exposure, sets the QD areal density across three orders of magnitude, from 10$^2$ to 10$^5$ $μm^{-2}$, covering both isolated emitters and dense gain media. Structural analysis reveals well-defined GaAsSb QDs with a mixed GaAs/GaSb composition and no extended defects. Temperature-dependent photoluminescence measurements confirm emission at 1550 nm (0.8 eV) within the telecommunications C-band, with characteristic QD-like temperature dependence. Because the QDs form on a lattice-matched GaSb surface in a single growth step, the technique offers a practical route to C-band emitters built into the GaSb/AlGaSb device family already used for mid-infrared sources and detectors.

articles.title: Low-Field J-Coupling Spectroscopy Measured with a Diamond Nitrogen Vacancy Spectrometer
articles.abstract: Nitrogen vacancy centers in diamond (NVs) are point defects well suited to quantum sensing of magnetic fields. NV spin states can be initialized and read out optically with high spatial resolution, enabling detection of pL-scale volumes of nuclear spins. Using Coherently Averaged Synchronized Readout (CASR), standard NMR spectroscopy techniques such as free decay, spin echo, and PGSE have been performed with Hz-scale spectral resolution using NV-diamond sensors. However, using NV detection for conventional high-resolution NMR at multi-tesla fields is challenging due to the need to manipulate NV electronic spins at resonance frequencies 100 GHz or higher. Low-field J-coupling spectroscopy provides an alternative path to chemical resolution in a regime more easily accessible to NVs. Here, we demonstrate homonuclear and heteronuclear J-coupling spectroscopy using an NV-NMR spectrometer based on permanent magnets operating at $\sim$890 kHz proton Larmor frequency (bias magnetic field $\sim$21 mT). This field strength enables chemical characterization based on J-coupling using sequences such as Synchronized Echo (SyncE) and Spin-Echo Double Resonance (SEDOR), which do not require the strong chemical shift dispersion and pristine field homogeneity of high-field NMR. The frequency range is easily detected by NVs using standard XY dynamical decoupling sequences and is well-suited for applying Overhauser DNP, which can boost proton signal by two orders of magnitude. We acquire initial NV-NMR measurements of T$_1$, T$_2$, and Overhauser DNP in glycerol before advancing to SEDOR spectroscopy of methanol-$^{13}$C and a methanol-$^{13}$C/acetonitrile-2-$^{13}$C mixture at sample volumes $\sim$50 pL, in which we demonstrate measurement of $^1J_\text{CH}$ couplings and resolution between species. We also acquire a homonuclear J-coupling spectrum of a natural-abundance propylene carbonate sample.

articles.title: Microphase Separation and Ionic Aggregation in Oppositely Charged End-Functionalized Polymer Blends
articles.abstract: We study the phase behavior of binary blends of polymers with oppositely charged termini using an ion-correlation-augmented self-consistent field theory (IC-SCFT). Under the low dielectric conditions typical for organic polymer melts, strong ion correlations drive association of multiple chain ends, leading to emergent multichain architectures that go beyond a simple ion-paired diblock copolymer picture previously used to interpret recent experiments. At moderate to strong polymer segregation, the resulting phase diagram differs considerably from this effective-diblock prediction: ion clustering broadens the lamellar and cylindrical windows while suppressing the network phases, the reverse of the trend for end-charged diblock copolymers. At weak segregation, the two polymers remain miscible even as ion clustering persists, and decreasing chain length drives the clusters themselves through a sphere-to-cylinder-to-lamella shape transition, connecting continuously to the aggregation behavior of classical terminally charged ionomers in the limit when one of the polymer species shrinks to just the charged end. These results reveal that ion clustering -- beyond simple pairwise bonding -- shapes the self-assembly of end-charged polymer blends.

articles.title: Grain Boundary Character Governs Lithium Deposition Uniformity on Polycrystalline Copper
articles.abstract: In anode-free Li metal batteries, a bare current collector must be converted into a reversible Li metal anode during the first charge, making Li nucleation decisive for reversibility. However, how current collector microstructure governs Li nucleation and growth remains poorly understood, since prior studies focused on single-crystal surfaces to identify favorable crystallographic orientations, leaving grain boundaries unexplored. Here, we identify grain boundary density and character in copper current collectors as key regulators of Li deposition uniformity. Systematic annealing decouples grain size from surface chemistry, revealing that deposition uniformity improves with copper grain coarsening but saturates as disordered boundaries are eliminated during grain growth, leaving predominantly low-energy configurations. Atomistic simulations show disordered boundaries impose high barriers to Li adatom migration, whereas ordered boundaries and adjacent low-index terraces provide low-barrier pathways for redistribution. Copper foils engineered beyond this threshold sustain uniform Li plating across diverse electrolytes and improve cyclability in anode-free cells.

articles.title: Overcoming Indium-Tin-Oxide Optical Losses in InAs Colloidal Quantum-Dot Light-Emitting Diodes at 1550 nm
articles.abstract: Light-emitting diodes (LEDs) based on colloidal InAs quantum dots (QDs) have emerged as promising light sources for the short-wave infrared (SWIR) range. However, their development is limited by relatively low photoluminescence quantum yield as well as intrinsic device design challenges. Here, we report LEDs with electroluminescence (EL) in the SWIR based on InAs/ZnSe core/shell colloidal QDs, synthesized via a seedless one-pot approach that enables the rapid growth of relatively large InAs cores. Zirconium-doped indium oxide (InZrO) was used as the bottom transparent electrode owing to its significantly higher infrared transparency compared to the commonly employed tin-doped indium oxide (ITO). These two key innovations pushed the EL beyond 1500 nm, with external quantum efficiencies of 3.0, 1.2, and 0.6% at 1093, 1198, and 1547 nm, respectively.

articles.title: Pressure-Driven Topological Reconfiguration toward Fast-Charging Hard Carbon with Plateau-Capacity Retention
articles.abstract: Conventional carbonization of semi-coke induces excessive ordering of aromatic skeletons, producing dense graphitic structures that hinder Na+ intercalation and suppress low-potential plateau capacity. Here, we develop a rapid thermomechanical coupling sintering strategy using moderate pressure to drive π–π interactions and topological reconfiguration of aromatic units. This process suppresses excessive graphitization while constructing interconnected, twisted pseudo-graphitic domains with abundant closed nanopores. At 1000 mA g–1, PTR-HC reaches 80% SOC in ≈14.4 min and retains 90.1% of its plateau capacity, enabled by abundant Na+ storage sites and rapid diffusion pathways. Kinetic analyses reveal accelerated Na+ transport and a thin, NaF-rich solid-electrolyte interphase with fewer organic components. In situ XRD and Raman attribute slope capacity to surface/defect adsorption and intercalation and the plateau capacity to quasi-metallic Na clusters in closed pores. This work establishes pressure-driven topological engineering as a promising strategy for upgrading semi-coke into fast-charging hard carbon with high plateau-capacity retention.

articles.title: Vacuum-Evaporated Molecules with Giant Spontaneous Orientation Polarization for Inverted Perovskite Solar Cells
articles.abstract: Interfacial losses at the perovskite/C60 and C60/metal contacts limit inverted perovskite solar cell performance. Here, we introduce a vacuum-evaporated molecule with giant spontaneous orientation polarization, 6F-2PI, for simultaneously tailoring both interfaces. Incorporating 6F-2PI increases the work function of perovskite, reducing the conduction band offset at the perovskite/C60 interface, which facilitates electron extraction. Concurrently, its phthalimide moieties passivate defect states, suppressing nonradiative recombination, as evidenced by a 0.03 eV recovery in quasi-Fermi level splitting. At the C60/metal interface, 6F-2PI also delivers efficient charge extraction, improved interfacial contact, and thermal resilience. Moreover, its hydrophobic fluorinated units prevent moisture ingress. Consequently, this dual-interface modulation boosts PCE from 18.5% to 22.5% with exceptional device stability, retaining over 90% of its initial efficiency after 2000 h under ambient conditions. Furthermore, this framework exhibits universal compatibility across both vacuum-deposited and solution-processed devices and simplifies processing for mass production.

articles.title: High thermoelectric performance in n-type–cubic (SnSe)0.55(PbTe)0.45 polycrystals via suppressed ionized impurity scattering
Suppression of structural transitions in iron: Magnetic stabilization of the bcc-phase via defect control
The Risk of an H5N1 Influenza Pandemic
articles.abstract: The last 110 years have seen four influenza A pandemics, where viruses have emerged from mammals or birds with the ability to transmit and cause disease in human populations. Since 2021, a high-pathogenicity strain of avian influenza, H5N1, has caused a panzootic (pandemic of animals), with global spread in wild birds, resulting in frequent spillovers into farmed poultry and into mammals, including mammal species not previously known to be affected by influenza A. This has created increased opportunity for reassortment, mutation, human infection, and potential adaptation to transmit. The risk to humans and the impact are difficult to quantify but of mounting concern to public health bodies. Here, we examine the risk of an H5N1 pandemic emerging and spreading in humans and the potential impact of an H5N1 pandemic.

articles.title: Amyloid-β Immunotherapy in Alzheimer's Disease: Challenges and Opportunities
articles.journal: Annual Review of Pathology: Mechanisms of Disease
articles.abstract: Passive anti–amyloid-β immunotherapy has shifted from repeated phase 3 failure to reproducible, although modest, clinical slowing in biomarker-defined early Alzheimer's disease. We review lessons from first-generation antibodies, including inadequate target engagement, late-stage enrollment, and limited outcome sensitivity. We then compare second-generation agents (i.e., aducanumab, lecanemab, and donanemab) highlighting amyloid-β species selectivity, plaque clearance kinetics, and durability, and we discuss emerging delivery innovations. Safety is dominated by amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, likely reflecting cerebrovascular amyloid vulnerability, and requires timely baseline magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) screening; APOE -informed counseling; and standardized, front-loaded MRI surveillance with symptom-triggered evaluation. We summarize prevention trials in autosomal dominant and sporadic preclinical populations and consider prospects for combination or sequential regimens with tau-targeting therapies. Finally, we focus on biomarker-guided implementation: blood-based prescreening, confirmation pathways, monitoring of biological response, and treat-to-clear or stopping concepts, alongside unresolved issues of health-system readiness, equity, and budget impact. Registry-enabled learning is emphasized to generate real-world safety and effectiveness evidence.

articles.title: Manipulating the Rat Embryo: Genetic and Stem Cell–Based Technologies for Physiological Research
articles.abstract: Laboratory rats ( Rattus norvegicus ) have been invaluable to biomedical research and are well-suited for physiological analyses. Nevertheless, technical challenges in embryo and genetic manipulation have historically hindered the generation of genetically modified rats, thereby limiting their use for in vivo functional genetic studies. Recent advances, including genome editing and pluripotent/germline stem cell technologies, have substantially expanded rat genetic engineering. This review summarizes the historical background and recent advances in rat embryo manipulation and highlights the rapid development of genetic tools in rats, now catching up with those available in mice. These advances provide an opportunity to reassess the value of rats as experimental models. Furthermore, the combined use of mice and rats, exemplified by interspecific chimeras and comparative studies, offers new insights into conserved and species-specific physiological mechanisms across mammals.

articles.title: Consensus, Disagreements, and Open Questions in the Psychology of Misinformation
articles.abstract: Research on misinformation has expanded rapidly over the past decade. This review examines areas of consensus and contention within the literature on misinformation, with particular attention to conceptual definitions, measurement approaches, and theoretical explanations. We outline views on what it means to be susceptible to misinformation and advocate for assessing susceptibility by focusing on the ability to discern true from false claims. Although exposure to fake news is less common online than many think, we argue that misinformation—more broadly construed—continues to be a major problem. We review evidence on cognitive and socio-affective mechanisms underlying susceptibility to misinformation, including repetition effects, lack of analytic reasoning, political identity, and information environments. We also evaluate interventions such as fact-checking, prebunking, psychological inoculation, and accuracy prompts. Overall, the literature reveals several robust findings but also significant methodological limitations and theoretical disagreements that suggest fruitful future directions for misinformation research.

articles.title: State Cannabis Policy and Public Health Research in the United States: Policy Disconnects and Research Gaps
articles.abstract: Ongoing liberalization and legalization of cannabis policy in the United States have shifted the focus of policy discussions to how legal markets should be regulated to protect public health. We reviewed the scientific literature on cannabis legalization, mapped current state cannabis policies using the National Conference of State Legislatures cannabis policy domains, and conducted a scoping review of peer-reviewed studies from 2015 to 2026 that measured specific cannabis policies and health or use outcomes. Across the 48 included studies, evidence was concentrated in licensing and business practices, nonmedical adult use regulations, medical program regulations, and local control. Our scoping review suggests that retail availability, outlet density, proximity, and local restrictions shape cannabis exposure and use. Evidence was limited for product regulations, taxes and revenue allocation, hemp/cannabidiol policies, justice system provisions, and public health/research policies. Future research should incorporate detailed policy coding, implementation measures, market data, surveillance data, and stronger researcher–policymaker linkages.

articles.title: Akkermansia muciniphila attenuates macrophage efferocytosis to enhance anti-PD-1 efficacy in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer
articles.abstract: Jiang et al. show that Akkermansia muciniphila reshapes the tumor immune environment to overcome PD-1 resistance in microsatellite-stable colorectal cancer (MSS CRC). Mechanistic studies and a phase 1 trial support gut microbiome modulation as a promising strategy to improve immunotherapy in this common treatment-resistant disease.

articles.title: Divergent interplay between STIM1 and STIM2 sets the efficacy of central synapses
articles.abstract: Stromal interaction molecules (STIMs) are endoplasmic reticulum resident calcium (Ca2+ sensors that modulate Ca2+ homeostasis. Mammals express two isoforms, STIM1 and STIM2, but whether they serve redundant or distinct roles in neurotransmission remains poorly defined. Using Ca2+ imaging and electrophysiology in hippocampal neurons lacking STIM1, STIM2, or both, we examined presynaptic and postsynaptic functions of STIMs at excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Both isoforms redundantly activated store-operated Ca2+ entry and amplified presynaptic Ca2+ influx, sustaining neurotransmitter release by expanding the readily releasable pool of synaptic vesicles and accelerating vesicle replenishment. These presynaptic roles were synapse specific: STIM1 predominantly supported excitatory synapses, whereas STIM2 was critical for the inhibitory counterparts. Postsynaptically, STIM1 and STIM2 exerted opposing effects on glutamate and GABA receptor levels, such that simultaneous loss of both isoforms rescued postsynaptic function. Together, the findings show that STIM1 and STIM2 differentially tune synaptic efficacy according to synapse type and subcellular compartment.

articles.title: Early-life high-fat diet accelerates the development of vagal satiation signaling and predisposes females to overconsumption
articles.abstract: Overconsumption of foods rich in fats, sugars, and calories is a major contributing factor to increased risk for cardiometabolic disease. Ingestive experience with these foods can begin early in children, yet there is limited understanding of the impact of early life nutrition on the development of vagal afferent neurons necessary for coordinating appetitive and satiating behaviors. To address this gap, mice reared on a chow diet (control) were compared to those reared on a high-fat diet (HFDEARLY). We demonstrate that the vagally mediated satiation response to cholecystokinin (CCK) does not mature until adolescence in chow-reared mice. However, HFDEARLY exposure triggers a precocious maturation of this response, accompanied by transcriptomic changes in the nodose ganglion. Durable changes in orosensory processing and appetitive behaviors are also evident in adult female HFDEARLY mice, which consume more lipid and calorie-dense liquid diet than controls, suggesting a lasting, sex-specific vulnerability to overconsumption of palatable, energy-dense foods.

articles.title: Lymphangiogenesis driven by VEGF-C reshapes tumor immune landscape and enables tumor eradication by viral immunotherapy in mouse melanoma models
articles.abstract: Vascular Endothelial Growth Factor C (VEGF-C), a key lymphangiogenic growth factor, has been implicated in improving responses to cancer immunotherapy. We investigated the impact of VEGF-C on the efficacy of oncolytic virotherapy with avian paramyxoviruses APMV-1 (NDV) and APMV-4. Treatment of B16F10 tumors lacking VEGF-C delays tumor growth, and complete responses (CRs) are rare. In contrast, virotherapy of VEGF-C-expressing tumors leads to CRs in most mice. Rechallenged mice remain tumor- and metastasis-free for over two years, indicating durable immunity. VEGF-C-induced lymphangiogenesis correlates with high CD8+ and CD4+ T cell densities near lymphatic vessels. Spectral flow cytometry shows changes in the composition and activation of CD8+ T cells, CD4+ T cells and NK cells associated with CRs, including enrichment of CD8+CD25+PD-1+ effector T cells. T cell composition changes in sentinel and contralateral lymph nodes, indicating a systemic response. These findings demonstrate that VEGF-C-driven remodeling of the tumor immune microenvironment enables durable CRs to APMV virotherapy.

articles.title: NAD+ precursor treatment prevents cardiomyopathy but disrupts erythroid maturation in mitochondrial progeria
Neoplastic and non-neoplastic astrocyte states converge on mesenchymal and injury-response programs during glioblastoma recurrence
articles.abstract: Glioblastomas initially respond to radiotherapy but invariably recur, often within high-dose radiation treatment fields. Although stromal radiation responses are incompletely understood, evidence suggests that the tumor microenvironment becomes tumor-supportive after therapy. Using a genetically engineered glioblastoma mouse model, we profiled healthy brain, primary tumors, and post-radiotherapy recurrences with single-cell and spatial transcriptomics and immunofluorescence. Across 13 non-neoplastic cell types and 10 tumor cell states, we mapped transcriptional adaptations accompanying progression from healthy brain to primary and recurrent glioblastoma. We find distinct astrocyte states linked to disease stage, including reactive, non-neoplastic astrocytes and tumor cells adopting reactive astrocyte-like phenotypes. Reactive astrocyte-like tumor cells with mesenchymal and injury-response signatures are enriched after radiotherapy and persist in recurrent tumors. Receptor-ligand interactions between reactive astrocytes and tumor cells include known and putative drivers of aggressiveness. These findings highlight convergent reactive astrocyte programs in astrocytes and tumor cells as potential mediators of glioblastoma radioresistance.

articles.title: NKG2D overexpression potentiates CAR-T cells through costimulation by tumor NKG2D ligands
articles.abstract: Li et al. show that activated CAR-T cells upregulate NKG2D ligands (NKG2DLs), rendering them susceptible to NK cells. Overexpressing NKG2D shields endogenous ligands and harnesses tumor NKG2DLs for costimulation, thereby enhancing CAR-T cell persistence, tumor infiltration, and antitumor efficacy across multiple models.

articles.title: Targeting MMGT1 enhances immunotherapy efficacy in triple-negative breast cancer
articles.abstract: Liu et al. demonstrate that high membrane magnesium transporter 1 (MMGT1) expression promotes immune evasion via a senescence-associated secretory phenotype that induces CD8+ T cells exhaustion. Targeting MMGT1 represents a promising strategy to improve anti-PD-1 immunotherapy efficacy.

Organotypic vascularization improves maturation of human stem cell-derived islets and restores normoglycemia in diabetic mice
articles.abstract: Wang et al. generate vascularized pancreatic islet organoids (VPIOs) containing organotypic vascular networks exhibiting endothelial fenestration. Vascularization enhances β cell maturation in vitro and survival under hypoxia. Following transplantation into diabetic mice, VPIOs establish functional connections with the host vasculature and effectively restore normoglycemia.

articles.title: Bacterial Surfaces and Barriers: Biogenesis and Pathogen–Host Interactions
articles.abstract: The bacterial surface represents the primary interface between pathogens and hosts, yet its chemical and architectural complexity challenges conventional classification. This Review examines structural organization, molecular composition, and biogenesis of bacterial surface components across the Gracilicutes and Terrabacteria clades, linking mechanistic detail to pathogenic function. We describe lipid diversity, integral membrane protein biogenesis, and lipoprotein processing at the inner membrane and how these components support surface remodeling, secretion, and virulence. We then examine the peptidoglycan layer and its role in immune recognition and surface protein display, teichoic acids and their contributions to antimicrobial resistance and immune evasion, and S layers, whose crystalline arrays mediate adhesion and immune modulation. The outer membrane section covers lipopolysaccharide biosynthesis, outer membrane protein biogenesis and folding, lipoprotein trafficking, and contributions to pathogenicity, while the mycobacterial section addresses the mycolyl-arabinogalactan-peptidoglycan complex and virulence factors. We discuss bacterial capsule diversity, biosynthesis, and use as vaccine antigens, along with adhesive surface structures such as fimbriae, pili, and curli fibers and their roles in colonization and biofilm formation, before covering secretion systems types I through XI and their contributions to virulence. This Review provides a framework for understanding how bacterial surface diversity shapes infection and identifies chemical vulnerabilities for therapeutics.

articles.title: Mapping Local Environments in Single-Atom Catalysts
articles.abstract: Single-atom catalysts (SACs) offer exceptional structural resolution for investigating how local environments govern catalytic behavior and, ultimately, for controlling these effects through catalyst design. Yet, atomic dispersion does not imply a single or fully defined catalytic environment. The behavior of atomically dispersed active centers is shaped by a hierarchical local environment comprising persistent and transient contributions, while also being influenced by an extended reaction environment that intersects with the local environment in controlling reactivity and can become integrated into it. Establishing these boundaries and understanding how these contributions evolve and interact are central challenges in the interpretation and design of SACs. Here, we critically examine how local environments are generated and controlled, experimentally and theoretically resolved across spatial and temporal scales, transformed from synthesis through operation and deactivation, and linked to catalytic performance through structural, energetic, and electronic descriptors. By integrating aspects that are often considered separately and highlighting those that remain insufficiently addressed, we provide a roadmap toward the predictive, environment-driven design of SACs and a deeper understanding of catalytic phenomena.

articles.title: Regenerated Cellulose for Sustainable Electronic Devices
articles.abstract: Regenerated cellulose (RC), derived from natural cellulose through dissolution and regeneration processes, has emerged as a sustainable, versatile, and cost-effective material for advanced electronic devices. With unique hierarchical structures, abundant hydroxy groups, and excellent mechanical and thermal properties, RC allows extensive customization of its characteristics, offering biocompatibility, flexibility, processability, and environmental friendliness. This review systematically summarizes recent advances in RC-based electronics, focusing on its multiscale molecular configuration, dissolution and regeneration mechanisms, and functionalization and engineering strategies. It first provides a detailed molecular-level analysis of RC structures and formation mechanisms. The principles and strategies of cellulose dissolution and regeneration are then discussed, with emphasis on solvent systems and structure-regulating mechanisms essential for processing control. Functionalization strategies are categorized into direct modification and hybridization with functional materials. Notably, the hybridization approach involves the development of conductive, semiconductive, and insulating RC composites, evaluated from the perspectives of material selection, interfacial design, and processing techniques. Subsequently, engineering approaches to enhance mechanical strength, electrical conductivity, and optical transparency are explored. Applications of RC in sensors, actuators, circuits, energy harvesting and storage devices, and electromagnetic shielding devices are highlighted, demonstrating its potential to drive sustainable innovation in electronics. Finally, future directions are proposed to address remaining challenges, paving the way for RC to contribute to eco-friendly, high-performance electronic devices.

articles.title: Hole-selective self-assembled monolayers: a molecular platform for high-performance perovskite photovoltaics
articles.abstract: Classification of donor–acceptor molecular components used to identify key self-assembled monolayers (SAMs) as HTLs for overcoming efficiency limitations in solar cells.

articles.title: Layered superlattices: from physical assembly to chemical synthesis and emerging applications
articles.abstract: This review summarizes the classification, physical and chemical synthesis, and structure–property relationships of layered superlattices, with emphasis on emerging applications, structural control, dynamic characterization, and device integration.

articles.title: Liquid hydrocarbon separation membranes: mechanistic insight, material design and microenvironment engineering
articles.abstract: This review proposes a mechanism-based unified framework for liquid hydrocarbon separation membranes and discusses the fabrication- and application-oriented regulation strategies in microenvironment engineering.

articles.title: Density Functional Theory and Data-Driven Insights into Hydrogen Incorporation and Transport in Ternary ABO3 Perovskites
articles.abstract: Hydrogen is a promising energy carrier due to its clean and versatile nature, offering opportunities for decarbonizing diverse sectors. Hydrogen utilization in many applications relies on identifying and understanding materials with exceptional hydrogen storage and transport properties. In this study, we conducted a comprehensive investigation of the thermodynamic and kinetic properties of hydrogenation reactions in ternary ABO3 perovskites using density functional theory (DFT) calculations and machine learning (ML) screening. We performed DFT simulations for a diverse range of perovskites featuring a variety of A-site cations (Ca, Sr, Ba) and B-site cations (Co, Fe, Mn, Ce, Ti, Zr) across various phases (cubic, tetragonal, orthorhombic, and hexagonal). By computing all data at the same theoretical level, we establish a consistent framework to compare how crystal phase, lattice-site chemistry, and host electronic structure govern hydrogen incorporation and diffusion. Therefore, we identify hexagonal SrMnO3, cubic SrFeO3, and hexagonal BaFeO3 as particularly promising candidates, combining favorable hydrogenation thermodynamics (ΔG < 1 eV) with low rotation and hopping barriers (<0.2 eV), while orthorhombic phases, although thermodynamically preferred, suffer from proton trapping, highlighting the importance of phase engineering toward cubic/hexagonal frameworks. Ab initio molecular dynamics further support this phase-dependent kinetic picture by showing relatively facile H diffusion in cubic SrFeO3 but much slower proton motion in orthorhombic BaCeO3 under the same conditions. By incorporating spatial and electronic descriptors with the DFT data into our ML models, we further develop a mechanistically motivated ML model based on structural and electronic descriptors to screen hydrogenation thermodynamics across 111 ternary ABO3 compositions. This model led to the identification of two additional promising candidates, hexagonal BaPdO3 and cubic BaSnO3, which were subsequently validated by DFT calculations. These findings provide a foundation for the rational design of ABO3 perovskites and demonstrate the potential of ML-driven frameworks with chemical insights to accelerate materials discovery in energetic and catalytic applications.

articles.title: Direct Measurements and Analysis of Catalyst Diffusion and Reaction Fronts in Chemically Amplified Resists
articles.abstract: The propagation of both catalyst diffusion and reaction fronts in a polymeric chemically amplified resist (CAR) is evaluated by time-of-flight secondary ion mass spectrometry (TOF-SIMS) depth profiling, and is compared with the propagation of catalyst diffusion fronts in inert resist analogues. We report that catalysts display accelerated and highly non-Fickian dynamics in the reactive CAR, even when located well behind the propagation front, while simple Fickian diffusion is observed for the same conditions in inert resist analogues. The complex catalyst dynamics of reactive systems is attributed to two key factors: (1) Transient free volume following deprotection events, which is a long-hypothesized acceleration mechanism acting on the diffusion front; and (2) a newly identified plasticization process induced by inert, nonvolatile byproducts of catalyst photoactivation. We propose a physics-informed model of enhanced catalyst diffusion due to the independent contributions of these two processes, and demonstrate that this model coupled to a first-order reaction provides a reasonable prediction of both the diffusion and reaction fronts. Our study presents a critical evaluation of mechanisms that control the spatial extent of reaction in CARs, and suggests that quantitative models of the patterning process should account for the impact of nonvolatile catalyst activation byproducts.

articles.title: Assessing the Potential Distribution of Eriocheir sinensis Under Climate Change: Regional Contrasts and Spatial Mismatches in Terrestrial and Nearshore Suitability
articles.abstract: The Chinese mitten crab (Eriocheir sinensis), native to China and the Korean Peninsula, has established invasive populations with substantial ecological and economic impacts in Europe and North America. Anticipating changes in its potential distribution is important for invasion‐risk screening and estuarine management. We developed a global species distribution model (G‐SDM) and regional models for the native range, Europe, and North America, each comprising terrestrial and nearshore brackish‐water components. Future suitability was projected under SSP126, SSP245, and SSP585. Terrestrial PCA‐env analyses assessed changes in projected suitable environmental space, whereas MESS and MoD diagnosed environmental novelty and extrapolation uncertainty. Terrestrial suitability was mainly associated with annual mean temperature, annual precipitation, and distance to the coastline, whereas nearshore suitability was mainly associated with water depth, chlorophyll concentration, and sea‐surface temperature, although the ranking of predictor importance differed among regions. Predicted‐suitable environments in Europe and North America extended to lower annual and wettest‐quarter temperatures than those in the native range. Under future scenarios, projected suitability was generally redistributed towards higher latitudes, particularly under SSP585. Terrestrial suitability showed more pronounced spatial redistribution than nearshore suitability in several regions, and the two components were not always geographically aligned. Terrestrial PCA‐env analyses indicated greater retention of suitable environmental space in Europe but increasing unfilling in the native range and North America. MESS analysis further identified environmental novelty and extrapolation uncertainty in some future suitable areas. These findings provide a scientific basis for early prevention, targeted monitoring, field validation, and estuarine management.

articles.title: Balancing Food, Heat and Predation Risk: Seasonal and Diel Movement Strategies of African Herbivores
articles.abstract: Understanding how large herbivores adjust their movement patterns in response to seasonal environmental variation is important for wildlife management. We investigated how sympatric African herbivores with contrasting body size, digestive systems and forage specialisation adjust their movement across seasons and the diel cycle. Using high‐resolution GPS data from 16 plains zebra (Equus quagga; hindgut fermenter) and 8 tsessebe (Damaliscus lunatus; ruminant) between 2014 and 2016 in the Okavango Delta, Botswana, we quantified 24 h range size, 24 h displacement distance, as well as displacement distance and tortuosity across 4 h time blocks, and evaluated these movements in response to season, maximum daily air temperature and vegetation greenness. Zebra occupied 24 h ranges double that of tsessebe during the rainy and early flood seasons, but 24 h range size converged during the late flood season. Zebra travelled twice the distance of tsessebe over 24 h during the early flood season, whereas travelling distances were similar during the rainy and late flood seasons. At finer temporal scales, both species showed pronounced but seasonally variable diel movement patterns. Movement paths were generally less tortuous in zebra than tsessebe, although interspecific differences diminished during the late flood season and midday. Movement patterns also changed with environmental conditions: increasing maximum daily air temperature was associated with a stronger reduction in movement in zebra than in tsessebe, whereas increasing vegetation productivity was associated with larger 24 h ranges and increased tortuosity, with the latter response stronger in zebra.
